Mr. DOHERTY moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 180, to amend the Canada Temperance Act. He said:
There are several purposes for which it is sought to amend the Act. The first amendment is to make such provisions .as are necessary to make the Act applicable in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Under the dispositions of the law as it now stands, the Act is not susceptible of practical application in those provinces. The second amendment looks to the providing of a list of electors for use in the election for the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act in different districts. The difficulty that has arisen, and that is sought to be obviated, has arisen in those portions of the province of Ontario which constitute unorganized territory. The general provision of the Act is that persons who would be entitled to vote at a Dominion election if such an election were being held, are entitled to vote on the election for the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act. The lists in unorganized territory for use in the Dominion elections are, under the provisions of the law, to be made each year, unless the Governor in Council decides in any particular year that it is not necessary that they should be made; and in practice such an Order in Council is passed save in years where it is anticipated that there will be an election. The result is that it may happen, and it has happened, that where it is desired to adopt the Canada Temperance Act in any district composed in whole or in part of unorganized territory in the province of Ontario, there is as regards that part no list of electors in force, and it is necessary to have one made which may serve at the election for the adoption

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: of the Act. Under the law as it now stands, even if only a portion of a riding forms part of the district in which it is sought to bring the Canada Temperance Act into force, it is necessary to make a list of that entire Dominion riding, which entails a very large and useless expense. The purpose of this amendment is to provide that when an election has been ordered for the adoption of the Temperance Act a list shall be made for such portion of the unorganized territory as is included in the district in which the election is to take place; and, further, that that list shall be for the purpose of that Temperance Act election only. The reason of that last provision is that where for a purpose of that kind a list was made of the electors in only a portion of the riding, in the event of a Dominion election coming on in that riding, it did not seem proper that there should be one list for one part made at one time, and the balance made later on. There are, in addition, two provisions made to settle doubts; that is to say, provisions with regard to contestations of the election for the adoption of the Canada Temperance Act. These provisions declare that the superior courts of the different provinces shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine such contestations; and further provision is made as to the procedure, in substance enacting that any person entitled to vote at the election may attack the validity of the election, and that he shall be bound to advertise notice of his contestation during a period of two weeks. As there are no persons who have any special quality to be defendants on such contestation, it is provided that any interested person may appear to contest the petition; and power is given to the judge, in the event of more than one such qualified person appearing, to make such order as may be required for the consolidating of the defences or contestation, and such other orders as may be necessary to prevent the incurring of unnecessary expense as the result of multiple contestation.
May I ask if the conditions in the prairie provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, where municipalities are nor organized, are recognized in the amendment?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The provision is that the word 'county' in the Act, as regards Alberta and Saskatchewan, has the meaning of electoral riding.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: Mr. .Speaker, I rise to a question .of privilege. During the remarks of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Mr. Sam. You will have to watch me closely, because if I say something that is not a question of privilege you will have to stop me. I cannot do anything better than I am doing. I said that I had risen to correct an omission in the 'Hansard.' There is something left out that I want in 'Hansard.'

I never 218i

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. Hazen (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for the inspection and branding of pickled fish, for the appointment of inspectors and the making of regulations, the nature of brands and the capacity of barrels, and penalties for infraction of the regulations.
Mt. HAZEN. The purpose of this resolution and the Bill which is to be founded on it is to give an impetus to the pickled fish industry throughout Canada, more especially the pickled herring business. At the present time, herring put np in Scotland and other parts of the world -sell for prices far in advance of the prices that are obtained for herrings and other fish pickled in Canada. It is believed that this is due entirely to the absence of proper methods in pickling this fish in Canada, because the fish that are taken in Canadian waters are quite equal to those taken in Scotland or anywhere else. Scotch herrings bring a price of $10 a barrel as against $3.50 a barrel obtained for Canadian herrings. The object is to provide for a proper system of inspection so that fish put up in a certain way will bear the hallmark, as it were, of the Canadian inspector, and people buying this fish will know that proper inspection of it has taken place.
Will the Bill prescribe the character of the package?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Will the inspection be compulsory?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No; but we hope and believe that the result will be that after a short time those who put up pickled fish will see the very great advantage of having it inspected and bearing the mark of the inspector. As a result it is hoped that the prices obtained for this inspected and branded fish will be very much higher than present prices.
Will there Ibe inspectors named for this inspection?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspectors will visit
different parts of Canada where fish is put up. For example, if the inspector is advised that at some point in Gaspe, or Bonaventure, or in the Maritime provinces fish are ready for inspection, he will go there and put his mark on the barrel according to the grade of the fish. When the Bill is introduced it is my intention to move that it be referred to the Select Standing Committee on Marine and Fisheries, so that it may have the advantage of its details being discussed by that committee, and the opinion of the officials of the department presented. I have no doubt it will receive careful consideration from the committee, and if any amendments are offered in the public interest they will be considered, because although the Bill is, I think, very carefully thought out at present, there may be improvements made in it.
The pickled fish industry of Canada, which includes the trade in salted herring, mackerel, alewives and salmon, has been for years in a languishing condition. Dealers in many cases refuse absolutely to have anything to do with the cured product. The cause of this is to be found, first, in the poor, leaky packages of varying size, which are in common use and which invariably ruin their contents in the course of transportation; and, second, to the lack of a proper system of grading the fish, together with careless, unsystematic packing.
This Bill, as I have pointed out to the committee, is intended to bring into general use an improved standard barrel for curing and marketing pickled fish, and to raise the standard of curing and packing to such a degree that the cured article shall secure the confidence of dealers at home and abroad.
To carry out the provisions of the Bill, when it becomes law, a small staff of inspectors will be appointed and duly drilled and instructed in their duties. These will

thereafter form a sort of travelling school of instruction in their several districts, for barrel-makers, fishermen and other packers. In addition to this, regulations in the form of a book of detailed instructions will be placed in the hands of packers, etc., for their guidance.
How will these inspectors be paid ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They will be paid by the Department of Marine and Fisheries out of the general appropriation placed at our command.
Will any charge be made to the packers for the inspection ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not proposed to do so at present. The inspectors will thoroughly examine all pickled fish presented to them for inspection, while the goods are still in the hands of the original packer. If the barrel is of the standard size and make, and the fish are graded in accordance with the regulations contained in this Bill, they will apply to each barrel so conforming to the requirements, a brand or guarantee of quality, which will show the grade of the fish, the year in which the fish was packed, and the inspecting officer's initials or number.
What will be the cost of administration ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We do not think that the cost will be at all large. Some of the officials at present in the department can be utilized for the purpose, and a few other inspectors may have to be appointed who will not only act as inspectors, but go about the country preparing for this work by meeting the fishermen in the different sections; pointing out to them exactly what the provisions of the Bill and the regulations are and educating them on the subject in the same way that lecturers go to the farmers to-day and give them instructions in regard to agriculture. It is not anticipated that any large additional number of inspectors will be required.
Is the Bill the same as the Act in force in this country some years ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am unable to answer the question of my hon. friend, because I do not know the provisions of that Act. My attention has not been called to it.
Does the Bill provide for a standard barrel?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Bill and the regulations under the Bill will provide the sort of barrel that will have to be used in order that the inspector will be justified in putting his mark on it, showing that it has been inspected by him and contains a certain quality of fish. It will have to be a barrel of a certain quality and of a certain kind, because I believe the great difficulty in the putting up of pickled fish to-day is that they are put up in barrels that are leaking in many cases, so that the pickle runs out and the fish become rusty. The term 'rusty' is familiar to all of us who live near the sea. Our friends from the interior will hardly know the expression as applied to fish. Unless you get the proper barrel to put up the fish in, you can not be sure that the fish will continue to be of good quality, because when a barrel full of fish with pickle in it is sent about the country by train, etc., the staves work loose; the pickle runs out, and the fish are destroyed. It is largely due to that fact that pickled fish put up in Canada brings such a very small price as compared with the pickled herring cured in Scotland, wnich in very considerable quantities are sold in this country and on this side of the Atlantic for a sum fully three times as large as is obtained for pickled fish put up in Canada at the present time. There is of course also a difference in the method of curing.

Is the inspection in
Scotland done by the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The pickled fish industry
in Scotland was built up under legislation of this character. A good many years ago there was the same trouble with the pickled fish industry in Scotland. Under Acts which are somewhat similar to this Bill, but which I believe .also provided for a bounty, the pickled fish industry in Scotland, from being a comparatively small industry and one that did not give very large returns to those engaged in it, haB become a most important industry. This was largely brought about by the passage of legislation, the object of which was to give assurance to the man buying the products that what he was buying had been properly inspected, and that he was getting an article up to a certain standard of excellence.
At the start it referred only to herring.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. As a matter of fact, if this Bill 'becomes law, it will foe used
chiefly in connection with herrings. It mentions alewives. 'Hon. gentlemen know that alewives, also known as gaspereaux, are smoked and cured and sent down to the West Indies. There is very little sale for alewives ini this country. There is also a provision in the Bill that any other class of fish may be brought within its scope if it is thought desirable to do so. It will also apply to mackerel .and salmon; and it is possible that in the future, although it is not likely, because the shad is not an important commercial fish in this country, it may also be applied to shad.

If the Government
stamp is placed on a barrel of fish, I suppose that the Government will be responsible that there is good fish in the barrel; and if there is anything WTong with the fish, that the Government will pay the damages. It is something in the nature of a guarantee-like the Farmers' Bank.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If the Government stamp is put on a barrel, and if it turns out that the goods contained in the barrel are not up to the proper standard, it will be perfectly clear that we have appointed somebody as inspector who is not fit to perform his duties, and that he should foe removed -and another inspector appointed in his place. A great deal will depend upon the efficiency of the inspectors and upon the fidelity and care with which they discharge their duties.
Will the appointments of the inspectors be political?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The appointments will be made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Will they be political appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. The inspectors will be men qualified to fill the position. If we do not get men of that class, this legislation will certainly not foe a success.
Will codfish be included?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Codfish are not put up in barrels; they are dry-cured.
The hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says that they are pickled at certain seasons of the year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My experience with codfish is that they are dried sometimes in the sun and at other times by process of steam.

All these matters will be considered by the Committee of Marine and Fisheries when they meet. If, in the opinion of that committee, which is composed of gentlemen who have more or less acquaintance with matters relating to fisheries, this legislation should be extended to other fish, I shall be very glad indeed that the Bill should be amended in that respect.

What I mentioned to the hon. member (Mr. Marcil) was that in my part of the country in the fall of the year large quantities of codfish are caught. They cannot be sun-dried, and are pickled and put up in barrels and sent to the market in that shape, which is termed ' green-cured.' That is what I have in mind.
Does this Bill contemplate a specification for the construction of the barrels, which I think is a most important matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It does.
How thick are the staves to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not wish to take up too much time, but perhaps I had better run over the Bill section by section, that the House may understand the nature of its provisions.
Does not this inpection imply at the same time the proper curing of the fish?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

Some years ago the
department established curing stations and secured the services of some Scotch experts. I know that in the county of Gaspe the assistance thus afforded was well received. Will the minister maintain that organization?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will see at once that you will have to have something more than the right sort of barrel; you will have to see that the fish is properly cured.
And to that end you will have to teach the fishermen.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We will do that as far as possible. The inspectors will go through the districts concerned and will get the fishermen and those interested in fishing together to explain the matter to them. If this were in relation to the agricultural industry, we would call such meetings farmers' institutes. Similar gatherings to the farmers' institutes will be held among 
the fishermen. A certain amount of missionary work will have to ibe done before this new system can be brought into successful operation. These inspectors will not only distribute literature showing what the regulations are and what requirements must be complied with before the brand can be placed on the barrels, but will have to explain the matter by word of mouth and answer questions as far as possible, so that the fishermen may have complete and accurate information.

Can the hon. minister
give us an idea of the number of inspectors that will be required?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot tell exactly, but the opinion in the department is that the number to be appointed at the present time will not be large.
I have 4 p.m. had some experience with these inspectors

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman will allow me first to explain the Bill.
Before the explanation is entered upon will the minister please state whether this measure has been submitted to the Fishermen's union or any opinion obtained upon it from them.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so. I know that requests have been made of the department from time to time that something should be done for the purpose of developing the herring fishery to a greater extent than at present. And this measure will apply, as hon. gentlemen know, not only to the East but to the West. There are exceedingly valuable herring fisheries in British Columbia. In some places there thg waters teem with herring, but little use is made of them.
Are they the same fish as in the Atlantic ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They may not be exactly the same, but they are good fish. The only fisheries that are developed in British Columbia to-day are salmon and halibut fisheries. Very little is done with the herring. This Bill will apply to the Pacific as well as to the Atlantic coast, though results will perhaps be made sooner apparent on the Atlantic than on the Pacific. But it is believed by gentlemen from British Columbia interested in the fishing business with whom I have discussed the matter that there is a great future for the herring industry on the Pacific coast.
Sections 1 and 2 of the Bill are the title

and interpretation clause. Section 3 provides that the Bill shall apply to salted herring, alewives, mackerel and salmon and the barrels or half barrels in which such fish are salted and marketed. It provides that the Governor in Council may extend the provisions of the Bill to any other kind of fish. It may be deemed advisable to extend it to the codfishing industry, though, speaking subject to correction, from what I know of that industry I think that will not be necessary. Section 4 provides that the Governor in Council may appoint a general inspector and other officers for the carrying out of the provisions of the Act. Section 5 prescribes the form of oath of office to be taken by these officers. Under section 6, the Governor in Council may make such regulations, not inconsistent with the provisions of the Act, as to him seem necessary for the carrying out of the provisions of the Act. Section 7 enacts that the brand provided by the Act shall not be put on any barrel containing herring, alewives, mackerel, salmon or any other-fish that may hereafter be brought under the provisions of this Act, or on any half barrel of the same, unless such fish have [DOT]been cured and packed in Canada or on board a Canadian vessel. My hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux), I think it was, asked a question about the place of inspection. Section 8 provides that the inspection shall take place at the port or place where such fish may have been cured and packed, provided that when curing and packing have been performed at sea the inspection shall take place at any port oE landing in Canada. The system of inspection is as follows: Any curer or packer of the fish referred to, desiring to obtain the brand provided for, shall give notice in writing to the nearest inspecting officer of the number of barrels or half barrels of each of the kinds of fish named which lie desires to present to the officer for inspection. The inspecting officer shall require the owner or packer to sign a statutory declaration that the fish were cured and packed in Canada or on board a Canadian vessel or boat within the period prescribed for the various classes of fish by the regulation. The brand prescribed shall not be placed on any barrel or half barrel the capacity of which is not as prescribed under the regulations, and which barrel or half barrel is not made and marked in accordance with such regulations. When these barrels are presented to be inspected they shall be opened and the inspector may remove as many fish as
are necessary in order to gain the information required and to make a thorough inspection. If the inspection is satisfactory, the inspector shall place the brand provided for upon the barrel. Inspecting officers may enter curing places. Penalty for unauthorized using of the brand or the falsifying of official documents is provided, and there is a provision that barrels cannot be used without destroying the official brand. Forfeiture of barrels of fish may be enforced in case of alteration or defacing of marks. Section 20 of the Bill provides that in case of dispute arising between any inspecting officer and the owner or packer of fish with regard to the quality or condition of the barrels or the fish they contain, the dispute shall be forthwith referred to another inspecting officer whose decision shall be final, provided that no appeal shall be considered where the identity of the article in dispute has not been preserved. It is provided that the Governor in Council may make rules for re-examination. Penalties are provided for the infraction of the Act, and provision is made for the fixing of venue. Section 26 answers a question that was asked me. It is as follows:
Nothing contained in this Act shall compel any person to present for inspection any fish or barrels or half barrels in which they are contained.
It is provided that the Act shall come into force on the 1st of May, 1915, but the officers referred to in the Act may be appointed and regulations made at any time after the passing of the Act.
The reason for that is that it is important that between now and the coming into force of the Act the inspectors should be actually travelling through the fishing districts, affording the people information which they ought to have before this Act is put in force, of the actual work of inspection, so that the people may understand the proper steps to be taken.
Then, there is a provision with regard to penalties. As I have said, it is my intention to move, after the second reading, that this Bill be referred to the Committee on Marine and Fisheries. I think that most of the members interested in the fishing industry are members of that committee. Of course, the Bill is absolutely non-political, and it is desirable, in the interest of the preserved fish industry, that the gentlemen who are interested in it should give their best thought and consideration to the Bill with the purpose of perfecting it as far as possible.

Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Hazen thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 182, to provide for the inspection and branding of pickled fish.

On motion of Mr. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to grant from the first day of April, 1914, during her natural life, an annual allowance of $500 to Mrs. Alice Joynson, widow of the late J. H. Joynson, in his lifetime a guard in the British Columbia penitentiary, who was killed in the performance of his duty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Bill which it is
intended to found upon this resolution provides an annuity of $500 for Mrs. Alice Joynson, who is mentioned in the resolution. This lady is the widow of a man named Joynson, who was employed as a guard in the British Columbia penitentiary. Something over a year ago, this man was killed in endeavouring to prevent the escape from the penitentiary of two very desperate criminals. In their endeavour to escape, one of the criminals was killed and, very unfortunately, this man Joynson was also killed. I may say that his conduct on the occasion showed what I think may be properly described as conspicuous bravery. These two desperate men had succeeded, in the first place, in depriving one of the guards of the penitentiary, who was in immediate supervision over them, of his revolver, and then, by threatening other guards as they passed through different portions of the penitentiary grounds with this revolver, they succeeded in possessing themselves of the revolvers of those guards too. They had reached the final gates which separated them from liberty and were threatening the guards upon the wall when this man Joynson came to the rescue and at the risk, and, as it proved, at the price of his own life, intervened to prevent the escape. As I said, one of the two men endeavouring to escape was, after the intervention of Joynson, shot by the guard who was upon the wall. The other one was captured and subsequently tried |for the murder of Joynson, convicted, and hanged. Mr. 
Joynson left a widow, who is in poor health and has two or three small children. She is, as I am reliably informed, incapable really of earning her livelihood and has no one to whom she may look for support or assistance. It has seemed to us that this was a deserving case from every point of view. Apart from the needs of this unfortunate woman and her young children, we have been very much influenced by the consideration that bravery such as that displayed by this man in the performance of his duty calls for recognition. It would seem to me in the public interest that guards in our penitemitiaries who may be called upon to perform a duty similar to that which this man so courageously performed should have the encouragement of realizing that if, in endeavouring to perform that duty, they sacrifice their lives, those who are dearest to them and are dependent upon them shall not be left in want by their conduct.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I certainly
will not offer any objection to the resolution, -and I think the widow who is to be given this pension is fully entitled to it. Nobody, I -am sure, will question the propriety of the Government encouraging bravery such as was- shown by this particular officer, but I would suggest that instead of dealing with isolated cases in this way it would be better to have a general law providing that the widow and children of any man who loses his life in the performance of his duty shall be properly rewarded.

I do not wish to offer
any objection to the Bill, but I might remind the House and the leader of the Government that the Minister of Justice is more generous than the Postmaster General. Three years ago a mail carrier perished in trying to save the mails during a storm on -lake of Two Mountains-, between Ottawa and Montreal. He left a widow and five or six children. The case was brought to the notice of the House by the hon. member for Two Mountains (Mr. Ethier). He begged the Government to do something for the widow and children, but the minister refused. More than that, the people of Oka petitioned the Postmaster General to transfer the mail contract, formerly held by her husband to the widow of this man. The petition -was turned down, the widow has received nothing, and there she is to-day.

I certainly concur in
what the minister has said, but there is just one thing I would like to ask, and that is whether any provision is made for the administration of this money. It is quite possible that while this money is voted by Parliament it may not be properly administered, and I would like to bring to the notice of the minister the desirability of having the money put in the hands of a proper person so that it will be spent in a proper way, and perform the functions we hope it to do in the way of looking after this woman and her children.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I quite realize the force of what has been, said by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition as to the desirability of making some general provision for cases of this kind. We shall probably have to deal with the subject of these institutions very shortly, and I shall bear my right hon. friend's suggestion in mind. This is the method that has been adopted in the past; for instance, in the case of Laviolette, who was warden of St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary. The present case calls for immediate action and justifies our dealing with it by itself, pending the adoption of a general system. I am not in a position to give any information in regard to the case put before the House by the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). With regard to the suggestion of the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), I may say that we did consider the matter from that point of view, but on reflection it was thought that as our purpose after all was to give this money to this woman-not to constitute her a ward of the State-we thought we would allow the woman to enjoy in her own way the money that we feel has been honourably and fairly earned. There is no reason to apprehend that she will not make good use of it. The amount of $500 a year goes to the woman herself, and we are obviating the complications that might arise from the appointment of a trustee; and possibly it might be difficult to find a trustee to act gratuitously. The woman appears to us to be competent to be entrusted with this amount, and we feel that we can safely grant the money to her to Ibe used in her own way. We are giving it not as a gratuity, but in recognition, not of course of a legal right, but of a most justifiable claim on the part of this woman, and as payment of a debt of gratitude to the unfortunate man who gave his life in the performance of his duty, and for whom all
we can do is to make this modest provision for his widow.

Suppose this woman
gets married, what then?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Even in that case, the fact will remain that her deceased husband deserves this recognition. This is not done merely because the woman is in want. If she were not in want, I think it would be a proper thing to do. I may instance the fact that under the Militia Act the widows of those officers who die while still in office are granted an allowance of an amount similar to this, and all that is required of them in order to be entitled to this amount is that they shall not be wealthy. In this particular case the money is not intended as a mere dole of charity to an indigent person; it is intended as the recognition of a service that I think may be not unfittingly characterized as heroic, at all events as regards the manner in which the act was performed.
How are the payments to be made? Does the woman get the money annually in a lump sum?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The proposition is that the allowance should be paid monthly.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I agree with the minister in everything he has said, but I would strongly recommend to him the case brought to his attention by the hon. member for Rouville. It is not in his department, I know, but the circumstances are very much the same. Here is a man who lost his life in the performance of his duty. The circumstances may not have been heroic, but, after all, the case is deserving of attention from the State, which has benefited by the performance of this man's duty. If the hon. minister could prevail on his neighbour, the Postmaster General, to do the same for this man's widow, he would win the gratitude not only of the widow but of every member in this House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I shall be very glad to call his attention to what has been said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Calling his attention to it will not accomplish much.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. DOHERTY thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 183, to provide for the payment of a yearly allowance to Mrs. Alice Joynson, widow of the late J.

H. Joynson, a guard in the British Columbia penitentiary

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Mr. Doherty, Bill No. 175, to amend the Supreme Court Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Will the Minister of Justice please explain this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Last year an amendment to the Supreme Court Act was passed, the purpose of which was to remedy a condition existing with regard to appeals in certain cases. The difficulty that called for remedy was that it was held, under the Supreme Court Act as it stood previous to that amendment, that under the definition of a 'final judgment ' there was no appeal from a judgment which did not ultimately dispose of the case, even though it might finally determine some substantial right. The result of this holding was that there being no appeal from what in Quebec we would call an interlocutory judgment, a judgment which did not finally terminate the suit though it decided a substantial right, the parties going on after the rendering of that judgment to a final judgment, and having taken an appeal from the final judgment, were in the position that the judgment which had settled the substantial right was not appealable by itself, and that their appeal from the final judgment did not bring up that judgment. They found themselves with an appeal merely from the ultimate or final judgment, which was possibly the necessary consequence of the preceding judgment from which they had no appeal. The amendment of last year so modified the law as to make any judgment which in whole or in part decided any substantial right of the parties to be considered a final judgment for the purposes of the Act. This further amendment is now proposed for the purpose of making the amendment of last year applicable to pending eases begun before the enactment of that amendment, as well as to cases begun after it was enacted. The Supreme Court has held that that amendment was without application to cases instituted before the amendment of last year. It is considered that the provision, granting the right to appeal,

should be made applicable to all pending cases without distinction betwieen those which were begun before the passing of the amendment and those "which were begun subsequently. The judges in a particular case seem to have held this amendment inapplicable, not , by reason of .any opinion on their part that it should not propetrly apply, but merely because they considered themselves bound by judgments that had been rendered in previous cases with regard to analogous situations. One of the judges expressed himself that he would be inclined to treat the amendment of last year as applicable, were it not for these judgments. From the point of view of what is desirable, I think this amendment ought to be recognized as applicable to pending cases. There is an addition which I think ought to be made to the Bill as printed. The Bill is made applicable to all cases, as well those begun before as those begun since the amendment, .and I think there should be an addition made to reserve the right of the court to adjudicate as regards costs.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will you require an enactment for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not clear that it is absolutely necessary, but I think it might be wise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think the
provision itself is a very wise one, but I do not think there is necessity for putting it in the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am disposed to agree that it is really not necessary, but I think it may be wise to preclude any possiblity that because the parties proceeding under this amendment succeeded as a matter of law, they ought as a matter of right, to be entitled to the costs. I move that the Bill be amended by .adding a second section as follows:
The costs of any appeal instituted before the passing of this Act in any such action, suit, case, matter, or other judicial proceeding, to which the said paragraph (e) of subsection 2 of the Supreme Court Act, would not, save for the enactment of this Act have been applicable, shall he in the discretion of the court.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House again in Committee on Bill No. 84, to amend the Export Act.-Mr. Reid. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
When this Bill was under consideration some time ago, it was suggested that there should be some amendment which would give the House of Commons control at the then next session imi respect of any regulations that might be made by the Governor in Council under the provisions of the Bill. I have prepared an amendment which is taken ipsissimis verbis from the Dominion Lands Act in respect to similar powers conferred on the Governor in Council by the provisions of that Act to make regulations in regard to important matters. It seems to me it would be proper to amend this Bill by a similar section, and therefore I move:
That section 7 as proposed he amended byadding thereto sub section 2 in the following words:
2. Every regulation made by the Governor in Council in virtue of this Act shall have force and effect only after it has been published for four consecutive weeks in the Canada Gazette, and every such regulation shall be laid before both Houses of Parliament within the first fifteen days of the session next after the date thereof, and such regulation shall remain in force until the day immediately succeeding the date of prorogation of that session of Parliament and no longer unless during that session it is approved by resolution of both Houses of Parliament. .

I do not think that this amendment, if I remember correctly, touches the point that was in my mind when I raised the question on a former occasion. Section 7 provides:
The Governor in Council may by regulation prohibit the exportation from Canada of petroleum, in its crude or partly manufactured state.
My objection to this section as it stands is that the parties who are to-day proposing to invest in the development of petroleum fields in Canada may be deterred from making such investments by this unlimited, unconditional authority given by Parliament to the Governor in Council to prohibit the export of petroleum, if produced. I iam not in -any degree objecting to Parliament giving the Governor in Council the right to prohibit the export of petroleum ; but I am pointing out the very detrimental effect that the giving of that right unconditionally and without limit must necessarily have on the minds of those whose money is necessary to secure the development of petroleum production.
What I urged before was that the exercise of this authority should be made conditional on the existence of specific contingencies, so that the prospective investors would know exactly under what circumstances they would be limited, as this section will give the Governor in Council authority to limit them. Perhaps I do not need to repeat what I said before. We think we are, or hope we are, on the eve of very large and important petroleum developments in Alberta; but those developments have not yet taken place. They may come as the result of a comparatively small investment of capital, or it may be that they will come only after the investment of a very large amount of capital. At the present time capital is being attracted towards those possible oil fields; and I think it will be very unfortunate if, by an Act of Parliament, we tend to deter the investment of capital, as I am sure the terms of the Bill put before the House will do. I again ask the Government to take into consideration the propriety of making the exercise of this authority conditional.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I remember distinctly
the occasion when my hon. friend put forward the reason which he has just now suggested. I found this difficulty in meeting his views as fully as I would have desired, that it is extremely difficult to express conditions in such a way that the section will be effective without leaving matters very much as they are at present. It might be suggested that we could insert in this Bill some such expression as that found in the Militia Act or in the Naval Service Act.
Yes, I think so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think it would be desirable to do that, and I will explain my reasons to my hon. friend. Conditions might arise which,, in the opinion of the Government, after consultation with the proper authorities, would justify some such action as this, and it might be undesirable, in the interest of Canada and of the whole empire, that the particular action of the Government should be publicly based upon the consideration which would thus be set	forth in	the Bill.
An explanation has been given in this House of the policy upon which the Government will exercise the powers con-ferried Iby this Bill; and, inasmuch as the Government renders itself amenable, with the least possible delay, to have its action in that regard considered by Parliament, I think that on the whole the proposed terms

of the Bill ought not to deter persons proposing to invest. I agree with my hon. friend in what he has said in regard to oil development, with a certain qualification. I would go a little further than he would go, .in this respect, that, so far as my limited 'knowledge leads me to have any opinion on the .subject, it would not seem to me possible that any very extensive oil development could take place in Alberta or in any other province of Canada except by means of the investment of large amounts of capital. A discovery of oil may be possible with the expenditure of a moderate amount of capital, if the discoverer happens to have exceedingly good luck; but the prosecution of the discovery of oil, as I understand it from persons with whom I have conversed on the subject on many occasions during the past summer, is proceeded with on thoroughly scientific lines-on geological surveys, and on the consideration of the elements which are usually found where oil is discovered in large quantities. Even when you find from the surveys all the geological indications that oil is present in large .quantities, it is nevertheless possible that you may not find it. Now, the prosecution of the search for oil involves a very considerable investment of capital, and, if oil be found, the carrying on of the business of production, as I understand it, involves, the investment o;f further large amounts of capital. A proposal such .as .this was discussed with some persons who purported to represent, and who, I am credibly informed do represent, large amounts of capital, and I did not find that they were deterred by the proposal that the Governor in Council should he invested with such powers as are set (forth in the Bill. That was my experience, and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche), who had even more experience in that regard than I had, derived the same impression from his. conversation with these persons. My hon. friend from Edmonton and I have precisely the same object in view. It seemed to me that, for the reasons I have indicated, it would be reasonable that we should meet his views, as provided in this .amendment; for no government would for a moment think of placing itself in a position to take action of this kind except for the gravest possible reasons. There is another consideration that I may mention: no government would undertake to exercise powers such as these 
unless there was need of that particular product (for very important purposes. It .seems to me that that consideration should be .a re-assuri.ng one to those who .might be disposed to invest their capital in such enterprises. That itself .is a further guarantee. Then, the Government exercising extreme powers of this kind must have regard to private interests which, if affected prejudicially, would be affected for the common good of the whole country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The amendment proposed by my right hon. friend certainly minimizes in great degree the objection we on this side had to the Bill. It does not wholly remove that objection. Our difficulty in the case of this legislation is that it is impossible to conceive why the export of oil should be prohibited. Oil is a commodity that is coming more and more in use, and at the present time, as suggested by my hon. friend 5 p.m. from Edmonton, the development is commencing to be more general. New fields have been found in Alberta. These will probably be found profitable; but no doubt with a blanket of this kind on the .statute book men may think twice before they invest their capital in these fields; the question will be asked at once by all investors: Why does Parliament contemplate prohibiting the export of oil? As I say, not sufficient reason has been given why such a thing should be contemplated. We have had the resolution debated, we have had the second reading of the Bill and are now in committee upon it, yet nobody has been able to tell us why the Government thought of this measure contemplating the possible prevention of the export of oil. There must he a reason, but what it is. I do not know. The only thing stated by my right hon. friend on a previous occasion, was that possibly circumstances might arise that would make it advisable to prevent this export. That is a very vague reason, and the circumstances alluded to seem very, very remote. If that is all, it seems to me the Government is taking a large power in advance of time and for contingencies which may never arise. As I have said, for my part, though I object to the Bill, yet the amendment proposed will minimize my objection. For, if the Government exercise the powers given them by the Bill to prevent the export of oil, their action cannot go beyond

the summoning of Parliament, and then the matter must be before Parliament and the entire subject will come up for review. That is a safeguard which ought to be effective.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps if the Bill should be reported and allowed to stand over for a third reading, I would be pleased to give further consideration to the views of my hon. friend from Edmonton, to ascertain as far as I can whether there is any danger that persons otherwise disposed to invest capital in oil fields would be deterred from doing so by this legislation, and I shall also consider whether qualifications such as have been suggested might be inserted.

I read in a newspaper
some weeks ago that the possible reason for this legislation was the prospective use of petroleum in connection with defence. The British navy, it was said, is going in for warships with oil-burning engines, and the taking of this power is suggested in case difficulty -should arise. In the county of G-aspe several efforts have been made to discover oil, and the discovery has been made. Last week I received a letter from one of my constituents saying that oil had been discovered in that part of the country at Port Daniel. I referred the matter to the Department of Mines to investigate, but I have not yet received an answer. Should legislation of this kind injuriously affect the development it would be unfortunate. Beyond doubt, oil exists in the Gaspe peninsula. The Geological Survey has so reported, and the latest discovery to which I have referred adds interest to the subject. Considerable money has already been expended in this matter. The reason for the legislation to which I have referred was only in a newspaper paragraph and may or may not be true.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I gave such explanation
as seemed desirable when I had the opportunity to discuss the Bill before. And I do- not know that it is desirable that I should say anything further upon the subject. I said that oil, so far as it might be produced in Canada, might be required for special national purposes, and that representations had been made to us from very important quarters in that regard. Oil has been discovered in more than one province in Canada. It has been discovered in my own province, in the island of Cape Breton, but up to the present time, I believe, not in
paying quantities. In Alberta there is strong prospect that it will be discovered in very large quantities. I hope it may be so. On consultation with my colleague, the Minister of the Interior, he corroborates my view that the persons who were here last year -and who represent, as we understand and (believe, very large amounts of capital were not disposed at all to object to the insertion of a provision of this kind, and will not be deterred from investing capital by the conferring of such powers upon the Governor in Council.

No doubt the Prime Minister is aware of the fact that nearly all the crude oil that is to-day manufactured into the finished product in Canada comes from the United States. This legislation is being enacted at a time when, so far as the -section to which reference has been made is concerned, it is not known whether there is a producing field or not.
It would appear to me, therefore, that this kind of legislation is not desirable, because, if the United States were to retaliate with the same class of legislation and put it into effect, it would cut off the Dominion of Canada very largely from a supply of crude oil. The Canadian oil fields are now falling off so rapidly that they are reduced almost to a minimum, and we are wholly dependent upon the United States for our crude oil supply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not proposed to exercise this power by way of retaliation, nor except under very grave circumstances which would be supposed to affect the public interest. The legislation was not introduced in this general form at first. It arose out of the fact that certain new regulations were made by the Minister of the Interior in respect of prospecting for oil in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. In the course of the debate, the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) pointed out, what was absolutely true, that the reasons were of a general character, and that the resolution should be in a more general form. This legislation had its origin in the fact tKat the Minister of the Interior, in the regulations lately established for Alberta and Saskatchewan Dominion lands, inserted -a provision of this kind with the full concurrence of persons who desired to invest large amounts of capital. But it was found that the powers conferred upon him by the Dominion Lands Act and other statutes did not go this far, and so we are obliged to come to Parliament in order to make effective the

regulations already established by the Department of the Interior.

I appreciate everything that the Prime Minister has said, but of course he will admit that there is an Alberta point of view as well as an Imperial point of view, and in any further consideration he gives to this measure I would like him to recognize that so far as Alberta is concerned there is a condition of emergency at this moment-that we are on the eve of great expectations and are very timorous as to the possible non-realization of those expectations. I would urge that, unless the empire is going to go completely to smash for lack of oil within the year, the Prime Minister should hold his hand until we see Whether or not we shall strike oil in Alberta.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will let it stand for a third reading in the meantime.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice) Bill No. 149, to amend the Criminal Code, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of this Bill is to constitute false statements, knowingly made in advertisements, an offence where the statement is of a nature to enhance or misrepresent the price or value of any property of any description or any interest in it. The occasion which has led us to 'think it was desirable that this Bill should be submitted to the House for adoption is that there appears to have grown up a very widespread abuse in connection with the advertising of properties for sale. Of course, every one understands that persons advertising will make the very best of the things they have to sell, and we do not

propose to restrict a man's good opinion of his own goods or his right to express it. But the Act proposes to make it a criminal offence for a man knowingly to make a false statement of a nature to deceive people as regards the value of the thing that he has to offer. I have had representations from all parts of the country, and I think more especially from the western provinces, that there was really a system of deception carried on in the advertising of properties for sale, such as townsites. A person under the law as it exists at present is of course liable for obtaining money under false pretences, and I would not undertake to say that if you can connect the actual obtaining of money with the false statements in an advertisement, you could not convict under that law. I would be disposed to think you could. The purpose here is to make it a criminal offence to publish as actually existing facts things that do not exist.

I suppose that
would cover the case of a man who advertised his goods as all wool when they were not, or the case of a man who advertised his shoes as the best in the town when such was not the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I should think not.
Whether his shoes are the best in the town is necessarily a matter of opinion, it is hardly a question of fact. People's opinions differ as to the respective qualities of goods. In the other case mentioned by my hon. friend if a man obtained money by saying that ' his goods were all wool when really they were not, I think he could be convicted under the law for obtaining money under false pretences.

My hon. friend mentioned real estate. Every one knows that many people-perhaps I am one of them-buy property without seeing it. It is well known that many of my hon. friend's friends have invested in real estate in the West, having been induced to do so by the prospectuses or advertisements issued, or on the representations of the agents. Is it necessary to pass special legislation to protect people who will go blind into buying town lots in the far West without seeing them? Does not the minister think he is protecting a little too muoh those who ought to protect themselves? Is it not a fact that those who deal in real estate do so moTe for speculative purposes than for any other? ,A man will invest money in town lots in the West with the expectation of a rise in

value. Does my hon. friend mean to say that this legislation is made to protect those who, for purely speculative purposes, invest their money in such real estate transactions with the hope of a rise in value in two, three, or four years, as the case may be? I want to be set right on this point, because I.have several actions to take under this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The object is not to protect people from going blind into real estate speculation, but to punish the liar who absolutely misstates the facts.
That would apply to a very large section of the community.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am not saying that a very large proportion of the community do that; but if they do they ought to be punished.
Does this amendment apply to selling anything whatever?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes. The man we want to get at is the man who deliberately lies. If they have no fear of the Lord, we want to put into them a little terror of the law.
It would apply to patent medicines and things of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It applies to deliberate misstatements of existing facts with regard to any goods.

I called the attention of the Government a week or so ago to a clear case of swindling in Montreal. A gold-mining company, incorporated by the Dominion Government, published advertisements in Montreal and Quebec about a gold-mining proposition. They held a guessing competition, offering to anybody who paid five cents, and sent in a proper solution of the guess contained in the advertisement, 100 shares in a gold-mining company in Quebec. The person who informed me of this told me on good authority that the first day after the publication of the advertisement 2,000 answers were received at the Montreal post office, the next day 3,000, the next day 4,000, and so on. Two or three weeks afterwards I saw the same advertisement in Quebec papers. This is a case of sheer swindling, such as some papers will not handle. A certain number of patent medicine proprietors would pay almost any price to a newspaper that would publish their advertisements. Would the case I have mentioned come under this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I should think it is a clear case of obtaining money by false pretenses, that is, if there is no gold mine in existence and the facts have been deliberately misstated. I am not certain that such a case would not come under the law as it exists at present; it verges very closely on a gambling transaction, but I could not pronounce definitely on that without looking into it. The new law we are proposing would certainly cover the case mentioned by the hon. gentleman if the advertisement contained any false statements as to existing facts.
The distribution of circulars would not be covered by this?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I take it that the distribution of circulars is one method of advertising.

I would like to read for the benefit of the minister, who is a good French scholar, a copy of a circular sent to me by friends in Montreal to show to what use the Montreal post office is being put:
Firmness-Audacity.	Success-Happiness.
French Scientific Bureau.
P.O. Box 169, Hochelaga, Montreal, Canada.
Audaces fortuna juvat.
Montreal, Canada.

I have reasons to beldeve that this circular has been distributed by thousands in the working centres of Montreal and as it is ,a pure case of swindling, I thought it my duty to call the attention of the Government and especially the Postmaster General to it.
