speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You cannot expect me to say offhand what provision of the Criminal Code already in existence is applicable to a case of that kind. I am disposed to think that if on the statement made money wa3 obtained, under the law as it stands now there might be a conviction for obtaining money under false pretenses. In so far as this circular might be said to contain a statement of something as being a fact which is not a fact, I think it would come under this Act. I do not know that it is humanly possible to make legislation that will prevent people exaggerating the qualities of the goods which they offer to sell provided they keep within the limits of an expression of opinion and provided they do not undertake directly and knowingly to misrepresent the facts. I do not know that I could say very much more in regard to that circular. I shall be glad to call the attention of my hon. friend the Postmaster General to what the hon. member has said.

I thought it my duty to read this circular, because the gentleman who sent it to me takes a great interest

in protecting the working classes and the innocent girls who -axe being swindled.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We passed some legislation last session in regard to -advertisements of certain medical preparations, and I -am inclined to think that a careful examination of the document would show that it came within the provisions of that legislation.

Would the provisions
of this Bill apply to those who make false representations during political campaigns?
Not unless they sell their services.

During the election in Chateauguay-my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny) was there

a promise was made solemnly that a bridge would be built by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) from Caughnawaga to Lachine. As a result of that, of course, the hon. member for Chateauguay secured a large number of votes. I must say to the credit of the hon. Minister of Public Works that when the question was put the other day -by my hon. friend from Laprairie-Napiexville (Mr. Lanctot), he said that he had never heard about it before. What would happen if this legislation should-pass? Could we use it against the -member for Chateauguay who made that promise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid there are
several reasons obvious to my hon. friend why this -could not be done.

I think the Bill of the Minister of Justice is- quite right, but I think that one word should be -added to it. It -says, * or any interest therein, containing any false statement.' The false statement is a statement in words. The greatest falsity, as- far as my ob-s-ervation goes, has been not so much in words as in pictorial advertisements. We have had a considerable boom in real -estate in the county and town of Welland -and if there was any swindling, as to which I hope there was none, it was in advertising and picturing conditions that did not exist. There are many people in the -section of country from which I come who were perhaps not swindled, but who invested money in lands in the Northwest, not by reason of the statements that were made, but by reason of pictorial advertise-

merits. I think that if the section read, 'any false statement or representation,' it would meet the case. The word 'representation' would cover a photograph, for instance, showing a large number of factories, railway trains running in a certain locality, or street cars miles away from the centre of the town. If the hon. gentleman's Bill is to be effective, it .should contain not only the words 'false statement,' but the word 'representation.'

I had occasion to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice, at the instance of the advertising clubs which have recently been formed in Edmonton and Calgary. These clubs represent the best newspaper men of western Canada, and they concluded that the .use that had been made of their papers had had a very bad effect upon that western country. False statements had been made touching the value of real estate particularly, as the hon. member (Mr. ('German) has just said, with the Tesult that many people are suffering very great hardships by reason of investing small sums of money in real estate on highly coloured representations, pictorial and otherwise. The Bill that had been passed by several of the states of the American Union was sent to me, but it went further than we could go in this country by reason of the divided jurisdiction between the provincial legislatures and the federal Parliament. The Bill that has been prepared goes as far as it is possible to go, having regard to the fact that expressions of opinion should not in any event be called criminal.
Is the newspaper held responsible?

This Bill aims only at persons who knowingly publish false statements.
iMr. MABC'IL: Do you not think that a newspaper proprietor should use some judgment as to the propriety of the advertisements that are published in his paper?

It is a rather difficult thing to say that a respectable newspaper man should be held criminally responsible in relation to every advertisement that, in the ordinary course of business, is handed over the counter and paid for. This Bill says:
Every person who knowingly publishes or causes to be published any advertisement for either directly or indirectly promoting the sale or disposal of any real or personal movable 219
or immovable property, or any interest therein, containing any false statement-
-is liable. I think that will meet the difficulty we have experienced in the West. It gives me much pleasure to say that this Bill has been promoted by the gentlemen who have charge of advertising matters in western Canada-not by any person interested otherwise, but by the press itself. I think the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Welland is a most admirable one, and if the Code, as it now stands, does not cover the point, it should be embodied in the Bill. I am not sure, speaking offhand, whether a pictorial representation would be regarded by the judge as an advertisement. The crux of the offence now constituted is misrepresentation as to real or personal or movable or immovable property by way of advertisement. I think that a picture would be regarded as a part of the advertisement. That view does not quite agree with what the hon. member for Welland has said, but in any event I think we should make provision to meet that case. What he says is certainly true in western Canada. I have seen advertisements sent down to eastern papers containing representations of new towns in which great industrial activity is shown, when, in fact, there was not a single smokestack there.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would be quite willing to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Welland. I have no doubt that a representation made by a picture should be treated in the same way as an actual statement in words, and even if it be possible that some other disposition might protect us in that regard, there can be no harm in inserting it here. I understand that the suggestion is that the section should be amended >by inserting the words 'or representation' after the word 'statement.'
Yes.

I am not anxious that
newspapers publishing advertisements should be relieved from any fair measure of responsibility, and I understand that the word ' knowingly ' is introduced for their protection, but will the minister give some idea to the committee as to how far that word carries protection? A newspaper is an organization for the publication of news, and for giving business publicity, and the individuals who constitute a newspaper organization may have personal knowledge of the falsity of statements contained in an advertisement. How far



would that knowledge of the falsity of the advertisement, on the part of one of the men connected with the newspaper, render the newspaper itself liable?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand the hon.
gentleman has in mind some company or organization that publishes a newspaper?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think an
enactment of this kind is intended to reach a corporate body, but I do think that any individual participating in the publication, with knowledge that a statement was false, would be liable under this article.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does not the word ' corporation ' include any person, under the Criminal Code.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not prepared to
say offhand. If you want to get a corporation convicted for knowingly doing a thing, you must prove that the corporation, in its corporate capacity, knew it. We are dealing with a very special case. The purpose oAhis law is to get at a person who knowingly publishes a false advertisement, and I do not believe it would be found in the working out, that the newspaper would be so much brought under this provision as the person who advertised. What it says is: Any one who publishes or causes to be published any advertisement. There is a sense in which a newspaper publishes an advertisement, and if you could get any individual who participated in the publication, with knowledge of its falsity, I think he would Ibe liable under the section, and I think he ought to be. If you could charge the corporation with knowledge as a corporation, and prove it, I do not know that you could not get at the corporation.
It is not directed primarily against newspapers; it is not intended to place restrictions on newspapers.

Under this a man is
liable before he has had any results from his false advertisement. I think this is very dangerous legislation, and for the reason that there are a great many such clauses in the Criminal Code whim are used by speculators and by people who rue their bargains. In my own practice I have defended quite a number of people who have been accused when the purchaser has rued his bargain and is not ready to stand by his speculation. In such cases, the purchaser endeavours to have the vendor restore the money by threatening crim-

inal proceedings, and eventually in some cases criminal proceedings are taken. I went this year to British Columlbia to defend a citizen of my own town who was arrested, though innocent, as innocent as could be, on a charge of obtaining money under false pretenses. It is next to impossible to .succeed afterwards in an action for malicious prosecution. When you come to take action against a person for malicious prosecution you are met with such hazy conditions that it is impossible to drive your case home. I do not know if my hon. friend from Calgary (Mr. Bennett) happens to have had that experience in his very much larger legal practice, but I sincerely believe it is dangerous legislation and liable to be misused by persons who have had the bad end of a deal. There is always a remedy under the civil law if a man makes a false statement but irresponsible people will grasp at a provision like this to have a person arrested and perhaps committed for trial, when there is not the slightest foundation for the charge. Grave injury is often done.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend is suggesting a case where a bargain has been effectively carried out. If there has been a bargain effectively carried out and one of the parties contends that he was led into the bargain and induced to part with his goods or his money by false representation, he may to-day prosecute before the criminal courts. What we are doing here is merely making it an offence for a man to publicly and deliberately lie, and scatter his lies broadcast in an endeavour to inveigle people into investing in worthless things, whether he succeeds or does not succeed; The evil that is sought to be stunned is an evil which in its effects
reaches a large number of small investors, none of whom will be sufficiently interested, even if he has the means, to bring criminal prosecution, if you leave the law in a condition where the transaction must have been actually carried out before there is any criminal responsibility. What we want to try to do, if it can be done, is to suppress the lying . advertisement without regard to whether the liar succeeds in getting something or not.

With what my hon. friend from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has said, I desire to associate myself, because his experience is a common experience in legal practice. But the hon. gentleman has, I think, overlooked one line

in the section which says that the advertisement ' must be of- a character likely to, or is intended to enhance the price and value of such property or any interest therein.'
The mere false representation is not sufficient; it must be of a character likely or intended to enhance the value of the' property. That, it seems to me, puts it into the hands of a judge, in the case of any prosecutions under this section to determine that there has been a misrepresentation which in fact has enhanced the value of the property or is likely to enhance it. That is the essence of the offence-not a false representation or a false pretense, but a statement of something which is intended or likely to enhance the value of the property.

The hon. member for Calgary has referred to a newspaper cluh in the West. I might say that the rural parts of eastern Quebec, last year or the year before, were overrun by agents offering town sites and lots of all kinds in Regina, Calgary, Edmonton and Saskatchewan. Each one made representations that the town in which he was interested was the great town of the future, and so on. In my own riding to my certain knowledge, these agents drew considerable money from the people through these representations, without any further guarantee. I suppose those who have invested in those lots have bad no returns so far

Yes, the\ will have to
pay the taxes.
Mr. MARCIL. The minister has said that these are the smaller investors. He can not expect them to take a trip to the West to lay a complaint, and therefore those people who have been swindled out of their money have no recourse.
Practically all the misrepresentations made to these eastern people have been made by eastern agents.
They are western syndicates.
It happens that it is our land about which they are talking; but the liars are, generally speaking, eastern liars.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Bill does not endeavour to locate the liars.

I would like to bring
to the notice of the minister one thing in regard to this amendment. If this action is to be made a crime, then the minister is 219i
creating a new crime. It might possibly be a crime at common law, but it is now by this Bill to be crystallized into a crime under the Code. It is the same kind of a crime as obtaining goods under false pretenses. The minister, I think, stated that it might even be covered by the section of the Code dealing with that. My memory of the section is that the punishment meted out or the manner of procedure in regard to obtaining goods under false pretenses is not the same as is provided here. I.would suggest to the minister that, if he is making this a crime, the mode of punishment should be exactly the same as for obtaining goods under false pretenses. If this is to be a crime at all, it is a very serious one. The court should be the same and the procedure also should be the same. This Bill, as it stands, is placing too much responsibility upon a mere magistrate's court, because summary proceedings are provided. A crime of such a serious character should be dealt with by a Superior Court; at least, a man coming under this provision should be allowed to go before a superior court if he desires to do sc.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What I said in comparing the two offences was that, I thought, as we had now a very well defined doctrine as to what was a false pretense in the ease of obtaining goods under false pretenses, that doctrine would find its natural application in the determination of what is a false statement or representation under this Bill. The difference between the two things, it seems to me, is this, that the obtaining of goods by false pretenses deals with an offence that is consummated and carried to its ultimate conclusion, and whereby somebody is actually fradulently deprived of goods or money, whereas, here we are limiting ourselves to the attempt to do that. A man is to be punished here for his advertisement, even though he never makes a dollar out of it. As I think I said before, I am not quite clear that, if to-day an advertisement could be traced as being the direct and immediate cause or the means whereby the person advertising obtained property from another individual, and if the statement upon which he obtained the property could be proven to be false, he could not be prosecuted under the law as it now stands. I am inclined to believe that he could. The purpose of this Bill is to make the false advertising, in itself and by itself, without regard to its successful or unsuccessful re-

suits, an offence. Therefore I think we may fairly differentiate between what after all is an attempt fraudulently to obtain from somebody goods or money and what is an actual accomplished obtaining of somebody's goods or money.

I am in favour of what the hon. minister says with regard to this section creating an offence, but I am afraid that the method of procedure to enforce the penalty, if adopted, is rather dangerous legislation. Following out what the hon. member from Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has just stated, namely, that a person who may feel that he has got the worst end of the bargain may take advantage of this section, I notice that it says that the man ' shall be liable upon summary conviction.' If we bear in mind what the procedure with regard to summary convictions is, we see how it adds to the opportunity for getting even with a person who may feel that he has been wronged. In my province-and the same thing holds good in the other provinces, according to my recollection-the procedure is this: If a magistrate has made a conviction and .we think the conviction) should not stand, the method of appeal is that the informant as well as the convicting magistrate has to be served with a notice of appeal within ten days. It may be that some person from one of the adjoining provinces is the informant. He comes West, lays an information, and, as soon as he gets a conviction, goes back East. If the person desiring to appeal cannot locate him, he cannot serve him within the ten days; consequently he loses his right to appeal; the conviction stands against him, and he goes to jail. It is true, he has a remedy by way of certiorari, but frequently it is very difficult to get a conviction set aside.
He is limited by the regulations.
Yes, he cannot go into the merits by way of certiorari; and, by the mere technicality of not being able to find the informant and serve him within the time fixed by the code, he loses his remedy.
Service on an agent will do.
The statute says personal service upon the informant as well as upon the magistrate.
Service on the agent.

I think the statute does not say that service on the agent is sufficient-

speaking from memory. If the statute says there shall be service on the informant, I think it would be well for the minister to consider that portion of the procedure and whether he could not be proceeded against in the usual way by summary or speedy trial, going before the county or district court.
The object is to make it as simple as possible.

But there is danger of simplifying to the extent of causing a man to lose his right to appeal. In my limited practice I have had a case of that kind. The man was certainly innocent, yet the only remedy he had was by way of certiorari.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If I correctly grasp the objection of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. McKay), that objection would be met if we made some amendment of general application with regard to the delay within which the notice of appeal must be served. With regard to the objection of the hon. member for Cape Breton, there is no doubt it is somewhat difficult to lay down any principle by which you shall determine what shall be an indictable offence and what shall be an offence punishable upon summary conviction. If we went through the code to-day, I do not think the method in which the distinction is made would indicate any principle. As is said by the hon. member for Calgary, the desire is to simplify the procedure, not to make this a heinous offence with extremely severe penalty, but to make it a matter of prosecution before a Criminal Court and provide what is a relatively mild punishment, enforcable in a proper, and we hope, effectual way.
It is as a deterrent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the hon. member
suggests, I think that what most of us look to in this measure is its deterrent effect- bringing it home to people that they must not recklessly say anything and everything in an advertisement, but that in their statements of fact they must keep within the limits of the truth-that they must not, in their desire to laud their goods or property, overstep the limits in statements of fact. Of course, there would be a wide field left of exaggeration of their appreciation of the value or advantages of the goods or property they have to offer.

Once you admit the principle of the amendment I do not see very much objection in the manner of working

it out; for the penalty is not very great. I do not see why you cannot trust the ordinary police magistrate-and most cases of this kind will come before police magistrates-to settle the question whether misrepresentation was made as well as a jury. I would as soon have the decision of an ordinary police magistrate as that of a jury in such a matter. As to the objections of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. McKay), that difficulty will be thrown in the way of appeals, I think the policy should be to discourage appeals. The object, as the minister says, is to provide a deterrent of false statement. I think the Bill is nearly all right.
I desire to ask a question. It is a very common thing to advertise a fire sale which is not a fire sale at all but is merely so-called in order to draw the crowd.
Not without some fire.
No fire whatever-simply open up a store, put in a brand new stock of goods, and advertise a ' fire sale.'
That is among western people, not eastern people.

That is not a compliment to the morals of eastern people; if they do not do it, it is only because they are slow. But is anybody hurt by such a thing? The people go there and get better goods than if there had been a fire. Yet, the seller has made a false statement to 'promote a sale/ which is forbidden under the Bill. It is not to 'enhance value' but to ' promote a sale.' But though he is not doing any harm, he would be in violation of this proposed law.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is there any section of the people who would rather have goods that have been through a fire?

They think they get
better bargains, and so go to the store. The sale is promoted in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I had not conceived of the existence of such a thing.

You do not want to put a premium upon lying.

The House in Committee on Bill No. 132, respecting W. C. Edwards and Company, Limited.

Mr. Fripp.	Mr. Blondini in the
Chair.

In the absence of the Chairman of the Private Bills Committee and [DOT]at his request I have been asked to explain the situation of this Bill. When it was before the Private Bills Committee, there was a very considerable discussion. Mr. Pope, secretary of the Hydro-Electric Commission, was there and also the Mayor of Ottawa, Senator Edwards and his solicitor. After a considerable amount of discussion certain amendments were agreed to, and it was finally left to the chairman to put the amendments in shape with the parties interested. But it appears after further consideration, that wha't was intended by the committee has not been accomplished by the amendment. In so far a3 the province of Ontario is concerned, the Bill is now made subject to all provincial laws and municipal regulations existing and it was intended that the company should also he made subject to laws existing in other provinces. But it has been found that there are no such laws in some of the other provinces. In submitting that amend-
	.
ment, first the provisions of paragraph 5a were amended and this language was struck out ' and subject to the provisions of section 247 of the Railway Act.' Under that section it is necessary to secure the consent of the municipal council by by-law. That feature has entirely been wiped out in the belief, as the committee had thought, that the language that was inserted, namely, that the exercise of the right should he subject to provincial authority and municipal regulations, would meet the case. But I understand there are no such regulations in some of the provinces. For that reason the company now can go upon the highways of any municipality in any province, except Ontario, and without even the consent of the municipal council, to say nothing of a vote of the people, string a line of poles and distribute electric current for light, heat and power. The promoters of the Bill made no objection to its being referred back to the committee for further consideration, and I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Fisher, that the committee rise and report progress. I understand that later on I will have an opportunity of moving that the Bill be referred back to the committee for further consideration.
Have those who appeared for the W. 0. Edwards Company before the Private Bills Committee had notice of the intention of my hon. friend and are they agreeable to it?
I am informed by the clerk of the Private Bills Committee that Mr. Green, the solicitor who appeared 'before the committee, is quite satisfied that this course should be taken.
What is the purpose of this Bill? I am surprised to hear about stringing wires.

The purpose'of the Bill is this: The W. C. Edwards Company, who were incorporated in 1892, principally as a lumber company, desire to distribute electricity for light and power, and the committee thought that, this power being foreign to the original purpose of the company, should be governed by the existing provisions in letters patent in which, I understand there is a standard clause which brings all companies getting letters patent within provincial laws and municipal regulations. That is the difficulty and therefore it is necessary to send this Bill back to the committee in order that the matter may be put right.

I was present at the committee when this 'Bill was before it for consideration. As I understand, any objection that was brought to this Bill was brought by the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario. The W. O. Edwards Company tried, as faT as they were able, to agree to the terms and conditions imposed by the Hydro-Electric Commission. It is a good commission, I have no doubt. I know very little about the commission except what has been explained, but I do think that in matters of industry, where companies come before this Parliament for charters, this Parliament ought to have the right to give a charter without having to submit to provincial laws. I would like to place myself on record on this matter. I do not want to make any objection to the motion of my hon. friend, but I do not think this Parliament ought to be altogether subject to the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario. It is a very bad precedent.

As one who took a certain amount of active interest in this matter when it was before the committee, let me say that the question is of the utmost importance to the province of Ontario, for which, however, I do not pretend to speak. But I do speak for the electoral district from which I come. That fact was recognized. The Hydro-Electric Commission were communicated with, and they appeared on the scene at once and maintained stoutly their Objection to the general character of the legislation. If there is any likelihood of this Parliament enacting legislation which will conflict seriously with the interests of the people of the province of Ontario, certainly that likelihood ought to be removed if possible. It is a very serious thing for Ontario, and especially for the district from which I come. We are very anxious to safeguard the public interests. They all come to the surface in this Bill. The objections to the Bill that were urged by the HydroElectric Commission were finally admitted and the suggested amendments agreed to by the Edwards Company, but, notwithstanding that, it more or leas leaves the question open. As to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Devlin) says, I do not know how far this matter may be settled. There is a question of interprovincial relations; there are legal relations existing between the provinces and the Dominion, but I can say that something ought to be done, if there is any possibility of a risk being run in this particular by which the Dominion
regulations, as embodied in statutes, may conflict with the public interests of the people of Ontario.
Just one word in reply to my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin).
I am not objecting.

provinces-the powers of the provincial authorities should certainly be safeguarded.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: An amendment was moved to this by the Chairman of the Railway Committee, and it was held over until the member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) could be here. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is opposing this Bill, but' as he is unable to be here to-night, I would like the Bill to stand over.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Although I am not authorized to -speak for the hon. member for South Wellington, I may -say that he told me on two occasions, on Tuesday -and ag-ain to-day, that he had no desire to participate further in the discussion.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
He did not speak to me to-day about it. There is a very important principle involved in the Bill, and this being Friday night -and not more than one-third of the members- of the- committee being present, I think the Bill should stand over. If there were not am important principle involved the Chairman of the Railway -Committee would n-ot have- moved the -amendment he did.
Mr. -MACDONELL: This Bill was three times before the Railway Committee and twice before the -Standing Orders Committee, and no Bill this -session has received so much discussion and consideration as it ha-s. The Bill passed the Railway Committee by a vote of twenty-five- to fourteen, an-d not later than this evening the promoter of the Bill told me he was -quite satisfied to take the Bill with the amendments.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The fact that the promoters of this- Bill assent to its going

through as amended does not mean that it is good legislation. I am not pressing that the Bill should stand, but I think it is-worthy of further consideration.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I was one of the twenty-five who voted for the Bill in committee, but I had not them -seen clause 7 which say-s that the railway shall cross only above or below a highway and that in case of dispute between the engineers of the railway and the city, the matter -shall be referred to the Railway Board. This clause restricts the Bo-axd of Railway Commissioners to putting the railway either over or under the highway, an-d they have no room to -use their judgment.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The Railway Board has
already given a ruling that the railway must go over the highway.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I was not addressing myself to the hon. member, who we all know knows more than the Railway Board; I was drawing the attention of the hon. member for South Toronto to the fact that the Board of Railway Commissioners are confined to ordering the railway to go over or to go under the highway, while in my opinion the matter should be left to their judgment without restriction.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is
right in his appreciation of what the Bill means, and that point was discussed ad nauseam in the Railway Committee. The object is that level crossings shall ,be put an end to in Toronto. The. city is now contributing over four million dollars to aid the railways in elevating or depressing their tracks, and when the work now undertaken in Toronto is completed there will be no such thing as a level crossing in that city. The cost to the city, to the railways, and to the Toronto Terminals Company, when the works are completed, will aggregate between -twelve million and fifteen million dollars.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would any of that money be applied in connection with this railway if it came into the city?

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not think it
would but I cannot say offhand. The idea is that there -shall be no level crossings in the congested area of -the city of Toronto. This line passes over twenty-four -streets in the two and a half miles it has already acquired as right-of-way. The intention is that this railway will -be compelled to go over or under the highways. If the engineers of the city and of the railway com-

pany cannot agree as to the method of crossing, then the Railway Board is to settle how the railway shall go over or under.
M>r. NESBITT:	My hon. friend from
Toronto (Mr. Maedonell) is always fair and reasonable, and I wish to call his attention to that point.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The best testimony
I can give as to this proposal being fair and reasonable is that the railway company have accepted it.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: We agreed to take up this Bill on the understanding that it was not contentious, and it has been found to be contentious, -and as it will interfere with passing the other Bills on the Order Paper, I think my hon. friend (Mr. M-acdonell) should postpone the consideration of it until Monday.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I thought the discussion on the Bill was pretty well finished.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: As I understand it, the Railway Board has already made an order with regard to the entrance of this road into the city of Toronto.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: They have made an order for the first two and a half miles of this road after it enters the city of Toronto, but that is only half the distance it will travel through the city. It enters at the extreme west, some five miles from the centre of the city, and they have acquired a right-of-way and have had their plans approved by the Railway Board for two and a half miles. That was in 1909 and they have not done anything since. They will doubtless ask for further approval of plans, and, it is only asked that this company be put upon the same basis as all the other railways which have been granted charters to come into the city of Toronto in recent years.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I understand that it is one of the functions of the Railway Commission to deal with crossings of all kinds. On January 28, 1910, in reference to this very railroad, the Board of Railway Commissioners made the following order:
That if the tracks of the Canadian Pacific railway are at any time elevated, then the tracks of the applicant shall be likewise elevated along the course of the line where the rights of way lie adjacent to each other, upon such terms as the board may direct; protection to be approved at such crossings as the engineer of the board may require before the road is open for traffic, and if protection is recommended at a crossing any other road is interested in, then the proportion of the cost of such protection is reserved.
Section 7 of the Bill says:
The railway of the company may be constructed across any such highway, or along any easement acquired for public works in the said city, but only above or below such highway or easement.
The order of the Board of Railway Commissioners distinctly says that, where the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have been compelled to elevate their road in the city of Toronto, this road must do likewise.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company have now been compelled to raise their tracks in the place of which the hon. member is speaking ?

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Board of Railway Commissioners have not seen fit up to the present time to compel the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to do that.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend is misinformed. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company are elevating their tracks.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
If they are, this railway will be compelled to elevate their tracks, so far as they are running along the Canadian Pacific railway. The order goes further and says:
That protection is to he provided at such crossings as the chief engineer of the board may direct.
Is it not more proper to have as the judge the chief engineer of the Board of Railway Commissioners, who, I presume, would be an unbiased judge, rather than the engineer of the city of Toronto, who would have a personal interest and prejudice in the matter ? If we are going to bring in legislation which will virtually be an appeal from decisions of the Board of Railway Commissioners and render void an order of that board, I am inclined to think that the board will be worthless. The city of Toronto cannot be more impartially looked after than under the order made by the Board of Railway Commissioners on the 28th of January, 1910. The board are very specific. They say that wherever they have compelled the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to elevate their tracks, this road shall do likewise. They say that, where there is more protection asked for at a crossing, the chief engineer of the Board of Railway Commissioners shall be the judge as to whether that protection is

necessary or not. I think we are going a long way to render worthless that order. In this case I am looking at the principle involved. I understand that the railway company is willing that section 7 should stand, but that does not do away with' my opposition to the section, because there should be some clear, well-defined distinction as to when we should interfere with the decisions of the Board of Bailway Commissioners. I think that is something which hon. members should consider before 'they adopt section 7.

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Would the hon. member allow the Bill to stand and let us go on with the others?

maintopic: TORONTO, NIAGARA AND WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I would like to get . the Bill through; but as it is requested that the Bill be allowed to stand, I will certainly agree to that.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House in Committee on Bill 150, to incorporate the Prudential Life of Canada.- Mr. Nickle. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-incorporation:

What is the purpose of
this Bill? Is it a new incorporation or an amending incorporation?
The object of the Bill is to give Dominion incorporation to a company hitherto incorporated in the province of Manitoba.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 7

continuance of officers and by-laws:

From statements made when this Bill was before the committee, and more particularly from statements made by the promoter of the Bill, who said that he would take no responsibility whatever for the financial standing of the company, also from statements appearing in insurance reports in Manitoba, I think the Minister of Finance should look into the affairs' of this company rather carefully before any license is issued, because the statements made and the figures given show that this company is as near dissolution and financial disaster as any company can well be.
I have received one or two letters on the subject.

I have no knowledge as an accountant that would enable me to ex-piess an opinion that would carry any

weight; but when I took charge of the Bill 1 asked that some evidence be produced to me to show that this company was solvent. Those interested gave me a telegram from Mr. Miles M. Dawson, an actuary of the American Government, who was employed by the Armstrong Commission when they made .their inquiry and also by the Canadian Government Commission. That telegram reads as follows:
I strongly recommend Dominion charter. Your company has ample resources to provide for all liabilities and a handsome surplus. It has secured a good volume of business with exceptionally low mortality and remunerative premiums, which are now sufficient to assure its success under a continuation of prudent and enterprising management.
I would deem it a favour if, before a Dominion license is granted to this company, the Finance Department would conduct the most rigorous examination. I think it only fair to the committee that I should explain that I have no knowledge of its finances except assurances from those in authority ,and from this actuary that the condition of the company is 'solvent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the request of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) is only reasonable in view of statements which were made before the Committee on Banking and Commerce when the Bill was under consideration. I have no knowledge whatever as to the standing of the company, because it has not hitherto had Dominion incorporation. It is a Manitoba company. The matter to which my hon. friend from South Wellington has referred was discussed at some length in the committee, and I there made a statement as to the course which would be pursued by the Finance Department before a license would be issued to this company. I think it only fair to say that nothing was proved, at least in my judgment, against the company before -the committee. There were assertions and counter assertions but the committee had not the evidence before it of experts on which alone it could reach any conclusion as. to the financial condition of the company. Prima, facie, therefore, we are entitled to assume that the compainy's standing is i&atisfaictory. But in view qf the charges which have been made yesterday morning, I directed a letter to the superintendent of insurance which I shall now ask to be allowed to place on ' Hansard ' because it beans directly upon

the inquiry of the hon. member from South Wellington as to what steps the Finance Department would take, before a 'license was granted to this company. I did not understand the hon. member to make any specific charges with regard to the financial responsibility of the company, but to say that from information which came before him it would appear to be not overly strong. Yesterday I directed this letter to the superintendent of insurance:
Ottawa, May 7, 1914.
W. Fitzgerald, Esq.,
Superintendent of Insurance,
Ottawa.
Prudential Life of Canada.
Dear Sir,-The Bill respecting this company was passed by the Banking and Commerce Committee this morning. As you are aware certain allegations have been made to the committee calling in question the financial standing of the company whose assets and business are to be acquired by the new company, the Prudential Life of Canada. As minister I was asked to state what would be the requirements of the Insurance Department before a license would be granted to the company and I made the following reply as to the action which would be taken by the Insurance Department:
Re Prudential Life of Canada.
' If this company is incorporated by the Dominion Parliament it will have two years within which to get its license from this department. Before granting such a license the department will visit the head office of the company and make a thorough and complete examination of its affairs. It will make a complete actuarial valuation of all its liabilities, examine its assets, and satisfy itself that its assets exceed its liabilities, other than capital stock, of every kind, by at least $100,000, that is, that it shall show a wholly unimpaired capital of at least $100,000.
* From the assets above mentioned there will be excluded all shareholders' notes for capital or premium on capital as well as all capital or premium unpaid or in course of collection and any agents' balances and outstanding premiums believed by the department to be doubtful or bad. Such assets as these are not allowed according to the standard of this department.
' We will also require that a deposit of $50,000 in Government or municipal securities or other securities acceptable to the Treasury Board be made with the minister, and all the other requirements of the Insurance Act and of its Act of incorporation complied with.'
Please see that before a license is issued to the new company the requirements mentioned are strictly complied with, and in this connection, as the matter has been made the subject of public discussion, I would suggest the advisability of associating with your own officers an outside actuary of reputation and standing in his profession. Please inform the member or members of your staff who may have to make the examination referred to of this instruction on my part so that it may by no chance be overlooked during either your or my absence on vacation or otherwise.
Yours truly,
(Signed) W. T. White.
I think it is only fair to this company to say, as I stated before, that in my judgment nothing was established against them before the committee. The committee, of course, were not in a position to pass upon the financial
9 p.m. strength of the company.
They could only do that with the assistance of experts. I think that the matter is now in such shape that any one who has to deal with the company will be entitled to rely on the Insurance Department having seen that the terms of that letter are strictly complied with before a license is issued. With reference to one sentence in the letter, I think it entirely unnecessary that any expert assistance should be secured by the Insurance Department, because I have the greatest confidence in the staff of that department; but as the matter has been made the subject of so much discussion before the committee, I thought it would place it beyond all doubt if the course which I recommend were adopted.
That is entirely satisfactory.

I am very pleased, because, while I supported the Bill in the committee, I moved an amendment that they should have $100,000 over all liabilities. That amendment was voted down in the committee for certain reasons, and I therefore congratulate the minister on the precaution he has taken, and I am quite satisfied that he will act in the interests of the people.

I do not think that the House ought to depend altogether on a letter written by the Finance Minister to his department. That strikes me as a purely internal matter between the minister and his officers, with which we have nothing to do. We have responsibilities of our own to discharge, and the question in my mind was in regard to the construction of clause 10 of this Bill. In clause 10 it is provided that a new company shall not commence business until at least $100,000 has been paid up on its capital stock.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. 179, to amend the Criminal Code.-Mr. Doherty. Mr. Blondin in the chair.

I would suggest to the hon. minister that the offence referred to in section 404 is so closely allied to that provided for under this Bill that there should be no difference in the procedure and punishment.
Carried.

The hon. gentleman
may know something about making nails, but I should think he should leave the making of laws to those who know something about that profession. Section 405 of the Code provides for the procedure and punishment in the case of an offence defined in section 404. Under the new law there should be the same procedure and the- same punishment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I pointed out before
six o'clock the difference that I see between the two offences. Section 405 provides for the offence of obtaining goods by false pretenses. Section 404 merely defines what is . a false pretense. The offence provided for in section 405 is committed when a person does by false pretense obtain money, goods or other valuable consideration. The offence that I am now dealing with goes no 
further than the attempt to do this. The offence which this Bill provides for is committed when a person falsely advertises with the view of promoting the sale or disposal of property. So, under this Bill a man may be guilty even though he does not succeed in gaining any advantage whatever. It seems to me that the difference between the offence provided for in this Bill and the offence under section 405 of the Code is clear. In one case a man must actually obtain something, he must get a benefit from his false representation. But in the case provided for in the Bill a man is guilty even though he may never succeed in gaining anything at all.

Would the hon. minister mind my asking him if it is not the fact that the Criminal Code and the quasi criminal statutes deal with the details of the moral law? That is to say, would it not be practicable and advisable to lay down in a general way a statutory enactment endorsing the moral law which we all understand, or are supposed to understand, and enacting that one guilty of the infraction of the moral law shall be liable to a penalty, say of imprisonment for not less than ten days and not more than six months? This being provided for the magistrate or other judicial officer before whom the offender is brought may say: I can find nothing in the Code to apply to your case, but you have perpetrated a fraud or infringement of the moral law, and therefore I send you -down for ten days. Carrying out that idea in detail, the crimes may be classed as of grade 1, 2, 3 or 4, and suitable penalties provided for each class just as in the Criminal Code, but, strange to say, though in this age we are getting down to first principles, even to defining primal matter, we have not yet got down to the necessity of enunciating first principles of law, at least so far as I am aware. The national law, the international law, the municipal law, and so on, all specify certain things. The criminal law in the same way specifies certain things, but I repeat that no penalty except what is laid down in the Scriptures is provided for an infraction of the moral law. I would ask the minister, therefore, whether he does not consider it possible and advisable to lay down a sort of open penalty which may be made use of when such a case arises for which there is no specified punishment. Many cases, we know, arise for which no punishment is prescribed. Men learned in the law will scratch their heads in vain, and turn up tomes and statutes galore look-

ing for some remedy which they cannot find, all because the general principle itself has not been laid down, and a penalty provided in case of its infraction.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggestion of the hon. member certainly opens up a very wide field for consideration. At the first glance, what strikes me as being the practical difficulty in applying the suggestion is that it involves the leaving to every magistrate the definition of what is the moral law, and what constitutes a violation. I am afraid we should find that different magistrates would take different views of what the moral law requires of the individual. I might be convicted of a violation of the moral law before one magistrate, and the hon. gentleman having the advantage of appearing before a different magistrate might be acquitted, although we had both done the same thing. It seems to me that is the danger that would attend on the adoption of the suggestion. However, as I said before, there is no doubt that the suggestion opens a very wide field for consideration and if the time should come when we shall deal in a general way with criminal law-and I may say that I think that time is perhaps very near at hand- the suggestion that the hon. member has made certainly will have the consideration that it deserves.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House again in Committee on Bill No. 114, to amend the Indian Act-Mr. Roche. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
On section 1-power to establish industrial, etc., schools:

There was to be an
amendment, I think, to that clause. I received a letter from the Minister of the Interior a week ago or more making a suggested amendment, but I have not got it in my desk just now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will let the clause
stand. The minister happens to be detained this evening, and I am not very familiar with the Bill. I do not propose to go on with any clauses that are controversial.
Section stands.
On section 2-taking land for schools:

I do not wish to delay the Bill at all, but I think this is really a
trivial reason for interfering with what should be considered the sacredness of the right of the Indian to his reserve. There are reasons why there should be such an amendment, but I think the reasons against it are much stronger. This is a provision whereby land on a reserve can be expropriated for school purposes. It is very desirable that there should be a school in certain places, but on the other hand it is very desirable that there should be no interference with the right of the Indian to his land.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman made known his objections to the minister?
No, we did not come to that clause before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member will state his reasons as fully as he desires, and we will then let the clause stand.
I am not insisting that it should stand, but I simply wish to put on record my views in regard to it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman
has some consideration which he regards as cogent, I would prefer that the clause stand in order that hi.s observations may receive the consideration of the minister.

I may say for the information of the right hon. gentleman that when this Bill came up the first time I took upon myself to read a communication from the chief of the Caughnawaga band, protesting most vehemently against any expropriation of that reserve. The Caughnawaga Indians have owned their reserve almost from time immemorial. It was given to them, if I mistake not, by Gov-enor Frontenac under the French regime. The Caughnawaga Indians consider that they should not be threatened with being removed from where they are. They are quite near Montreal and are practically white men. By referring to ' Hansard ' when this Bill was first introduced my hon. friend will see the protest of their chief.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As I understand the
object, it is to enable the department to provide facilities for establishing schools for the advantage of the Indians. I would not suppose that any very large area of land is required to be taken for the purpose.
Section stands.
On section 4-withdrawal from band:

There is a feature in connection with section 4 that I am afraid the right hon. the Prime Minister does not

realize. There has been a considerable traffic in half-breed scrip. I do not know whether that traffic still goes on. A halfbreed has the Tight to the issue of 480 acres of scrip. At the price of land it is worth a considerable amount of money, and there have been a great many withdrawals from the Indian bands by members of the bands, who are really half-breeds, having white blood and getting this scrip as half-breeds. It should be understood that a very large proportion of the Indians of the West have an admixture of white blood, so that really they would be entitled to be dealt with as half-breeds 'but they had chosen to be regarded as Indians and as members of the Indian band, which they were in all particulars except in the mere matter of some admixture of white blood. But in case they had a small admixture of white blood they were entitled to scrip. Therefore, speculators would induce them to withdraw from the band with the result that the scrip would be given to them, then sold to the speculator and the profit would be made by the speculator rather than by the Indian. The effect of this amendment is that when that arrangement is made with the man it will also be effective with his wife, if I understand the meaning of it aright. When the man withdraws from the band the wife is automatically withdrawn. It seems to me that when the man withdraws from the band and is given scrip, the wife is thereby withdrawn under the authority of Parliament and she will almost automatically be entitled to the scrip as well thereby doubling up the advantage of the scrip speculators.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Are the wives of halfbreeds, as well as half-breeds themselves, entitled to the scrip?

Yes, properly speaking,
unless the wife had white blood she would not be entitled to scrip but it seems to me that when you provide that, when her husband withdraws she must withdraw also, you are establishing a situation in which you would almost have to give her the same recognition as her husband. I am not saying that this is not right, I am not seriously objecting to it, but I am putting before the committee the information as to how far-reaching this provision is in a direction that possibly is not contemplated. It may be that under present conditions no scrip is issued. If the issue of scrip has ceased then the objection I see does not exist, but if the scrip is actually issued that condition would continue 
and I think it would raise considerable objection. It would foe well for the minister to look into that side of it before he puts the section through.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is quite possible that that particular consideration may have been overlooked. Apparently, as far as I can appreciate the object of the section, it is designed to ensure that the wife of an Indian when withdrawn from the band would have the same status as her husband.
Yes, which is very proper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Which is very proper-just as a wife acquires the domicile or national status of her husband. The considerations which the hon. gentleman has brought to my attention may have been overlooked. I shall ask that the section may be allowed in order that it may have the consideration of the minister.
Section stands.
Section 6 stands.
On section 8-selling, etc., of live stock:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Has my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) considered this section ?

I think it is going very far, but I suppose the minister has considered it thoroughly. It prohibits the Indian from selling his live stock. My objection to it would be that it establishes too great a condition of paternalism. It does not give scope to the Indian to grow in his sense of proprietorship, of personal ownership, which is really essential to his progress and civilization. The sense of ownership, after all, is the very foundation of civilization. Ownership, selfishness, which is foreign to the mind of the Indian in his normal condition, is really the foundation of civilization.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman considers that it tends to keep the Indians in a condition of tutelage ?
Yes

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Well, I think we had better let it stand.
Would not this go so far as to extend to the Indian, say, in the Maritime provinces so that he would not foe aJble to sell his live stock without the consent of the agent ?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is restricted to the four provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia.

It says:
No Indian or non-treaty Indian in the provinces of Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Alberta.
It might be construed to mean a nontreaty Indian in the four provinces and any Indian all over Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think it would be held to have that meaning.

It is a subject for consideration. I know that in the Maritime provinces there are some Indians who are trying to lead civilized lives and own property, and it would be a great hardship if these people were not allowed to dispose of their property.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think it does mean what my hon. friend suggests, but in order to avoid any doubt it might be proper to transpose the words of the section so that it would read:
In the provinces of Manitoba, British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Alberta, no Indian-
That will make it all right.
This only applies to live stock that had been given them under treaty,' and not to their private property?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

That is better, but it still carries the objection I have raised.
On section 9-restriction Indian dances, etc.:

As this section reads, it ostensibly is to prevent the engagement of Indians in public shows, except with consent, and I think that is proper, but if it is the intention of the department to prevent their assembling on different reserves for the purpose of participating in their festivals, religious or otherwise, that ought to be specifically stated, and this section ought not to be interpreted to prohibit that. The various bands visit each other on their reservations, to take part in ceremonies, religious or otherwise but that is in a different class altogether from their participation in a public show for pay. I know there are many people who object to allowing the Indians to participate in their tribal festivals and ceremonies, but, personally, I think it would be an injustice and a wrong to make a statutory provision preventing them from engaging in these traditional customs, to which they are much attached.
Mr. CARVELL.: An eastern man naturally wonders why an Indian should not be allowed to join a show and make a few dollars as well as a white man can. There must be some reason for this prohibition, and I would like my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) to explain.

The merit of the Indian is in the maintenance of his dignity, and when the Indian consents to join in a public show for money he degrades and demoralizes himself to an extent that would not be present in the case of a white man doing a similar thing. The Indian is either a gentleman or very much the reverse. As long as his dignity is maintained he is a gentleman and he is amenable to reason and argument and good influence, but when he loses his self-respect, and he certainly does lose his self-respect when he makes himself a public show, then he gets to a point where neither the Government nor anybody else can do very much with him or for him. There are exceptions of course, but I think those who are acquainted with the western Indians will agree that their participation in these public exhibitions has a degrading and demoralizing influence on them, whch is very much to their detriment and to the detriment of the Government that is doing the best it can for them. I am aware that very much of what I have said may be argued against permitting them to assemble in their tribal or national festivals, but in the celebration of these ceremonies, while they may look grotesque to us because we do not understand them, they have to the Indians a meaning, and they do not detract from their self-respect or from their dignity, and therefore do not demoralize them to the same degree.

What is the difference
between their dances and tangoing?

The difference between
the white man and the Indian is that the Indian is naturally a gentleman.

I endorse what has
been so well said by the hon. member for Edmonton. I suppose the intention of the clause must be not to prevent the Indian holding a festival on his own reserve.
Or going from one reserve to another.

Yes. The clause, I
suppose, is intended to prevent the Indians from taking part in these public exhibitions, and with that I agree, but if it should be interpreted to prohibit his national and

tribal festivals, then I think it would be harsh and unfair to the Indians. I do not think we have any right to step in and prevent our wards from indulging in these immemorial customs of their race. In so far as it prevents persons from engaging Indians for these public shows, the clause is a good one. Many years ago I happened to be in Ottawa from the West, and the man who had charge of the Indians in one of these shows made a failure of it, and the Indians were stranded. They made their way from some town in Ontario to Ottawa, and I happened to meet them in the corridor and I knew them and they knew me, and they told me their plight. I took them to see the Big Chief, Mr. Dewdney, who was then Minister of the Interior, and he had to take charge of them and send them back to their reserves.
I think the intention of this Bill is to prevent things of that kind from occurring. I hope it is not intended to prevent the Indians from exercising their old customs and privileges on their own reserves or from visiting other reserves. I do not think it would be fair to do that.

This Bill seems to prevent them from visiting other reserves. These people must have their pleasure, and if they are to be bound down so that they cannot visit brother and sister Indians on other reserves, they will be very apt to run away altogether. I suppose the department has in mind, for example, such festivals as those that occur at Banff. I have seen them and they are very harmless. I presume it will come within the discretion of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs to permit the Indians to visit other reserves. I think the Indians ought to be allowed to visit other reserves. These Indian dances are far ahead of the turkey trot and the tango that we have in Ottawa, and we permit these dances. If you go down to the Bussell House and buy a cup of tea, you can see white people go through these so-called modern dances that are much inferior to the Indian dances, as far as my judgment goes. Of course, I am not going to say anything against the people who indulge in these dances, because I do not want to step on any one's toes. I would be glad to see preserved and protected the rights of the Indians in their innocent dances, because I think after all they are as good dances as the tango and the turkey trot.

Of course, those who par-
[llr. Bradbury. ]
ticipate in the turkey trot and the tango, as has been suggested, are not doing so outside of their own reserve.

That is the very point I had in mind. In the city of Ottawa people are employed on certain nights of the week

I do not know, because I do not go, but I have been so informed-to dance these dances in public in the restaurants.

I was regarding the city of Ottawa as a reserve. As far as the purpose of this Bill is concerned, it certainly prohibits an Indian from participating in any Indian dance outside the boundary of his own reserve, except with the consent of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, or his authorized agent. How far it may be desirable to go in that regard I am not prepared to say, not having very much knowledge o|f the evils which are intended to be prevented 'by this section'. In addition to the reasons already adduced by hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the subject, it appears from the explanatory memorandum attached to this section that the preparation for an engagement in the exhibitions, stampedes and pageants alluded to, are very unsettling to the Indians; that the preparations for the celebration of these engagements very often occupies many days and, in some instances, weeks of the Indians' time, at -a season of the year which should be spent in sowing or reaping their crops, and that there has been a systematic practice of utilizing the Indians for the profit of persons who are engaged in getting up such shows. The main object of the section, as I understand it, is to prevent that. I do not know to what extent it is desirable that the Indians should participate in ceremonial dances outside of their own reserves. I have no opinion on that whatever. Tberejfoie I should prefer that this section should stand in OTder that the minister may make fuller explanation, as the subject seems to have engaged the attention of the minister and his officials In any case, the members of the committee will understand that there will be no difficulty at all about the Indians participating in these ceremonials upon their own reserves, and also that there will be no difficulty in their doing so outside of their own reserves with the consent of the Indian agent or of the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs himself. Whether or not a provision of that kind goes too far, I will

leave for the minister to determine and I ask that the section stand.
Section stands.
