speechtext: On motion of Right Hon. R. L. Borden (Prime Minister), Bill No. 138, to amend the Irrigation Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. IBlondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not very familial with this Bill, and I propose merely to run over it and examine the sections. Any that require discussion or are of a controversial character, I will ask to stand until the Minister of the Interior is here. Those to which my hon. friends opposite do not see any objection, if there be any such, may be allowed to pass.
I am very glad of that, because the hpn. member for Medicine mat (Mr. Buchanan), who is most interested in this matter, is not here to-night.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would my hon. friend prefer not to take the Bill up at all?

I have no objection to running through it, as the Prime Minister has said, and anything that we do not consider controversial may go through. Perhaps we would gain something if we ran through this Bill, as long as we are not committed to what we do not understand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Certainly not. If we pass any sections that are found afterwards to require further consideration, they may be brought up again.
On section 5-minister may permit diversion of water:

As to this section, to use a legal phrase, as at present advised, the section does not strike me as being such as I would wish to see. When an application is made to construct irrigation works with a view to securing a license to use water, as the Act stands the applicant must carry out his part of the contract, he must complete the works which he undertakes to 220
construct before the license is granted that will enable him to dispose of the water for which he has applied. But the effect of this proposed section is to allow him to dispose of water before he has completed his irrigation work-that is before he has carried out the contract with the Government requiring expenditure on his part. Suppose I apply for the Tight to take water and make a contract to construct certain irrigation works. Before I have half finished these works, I may begin to use the water and, though I never finish the works which I undertook to construct, may continue to use the water. That is to say I have the benefit of the contract without having completed it. It does not seem to me that that is a business-like proposition and I do not think it will work out well in practice. I have no doubt that the reason for this section is that in some certain case the applicant has found it difficult to complete his works, or completion has been delayed, there has been a demand for water, and it has been said: What is the difference?-we have got enough of the works constructed to allow a partial use of the water; let us use what we can use and we will finish later on.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Are these licenses for a definite term?

No, once issued, they are perpetual. That is the reason why, as the Act has stood, the licenses are not issued until the work is completed. This, it seems to me, breaks in on that principle, and I am afraid it leaves the situation in a condition that, I should say, would not be satisfactorily workable to all interests concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I suppose the object of this section would be this-
10 p.m. During the construction of the works, when partially completed, it might be regarded as in the public interest that water should be used for the purpose of irrigating a certain portion of the land that might otherwise have to await for a considerable period the completion of the work. I -see, however, the force of the objection that the hon. gentleman has mentioned.
Suppose the water were allowed to be used for a specified period.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I was just about to suggest that. Some words might be inserted which would subject the license to such conditions as the minister might regard as proper in the public interest, and also the

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
license could be granted only for a certain term. In the meantime, the section should stand, and the minister will take into consideration the suggestion made.
On section 6-minister may waive public notice:

I do not wish to criticise. It is, however, hard to know what some of these sections mean without an explanation. Probably the minister will look at ' Hansard,' and I might mention now that it would be convenient if he would give a short resume of the purpose of the Bill.
When we are at home, people very often ask us what changes have been made in these Acts. I generally make a practice of looking up ' Hansard ' for the speech of the minister on the introduction of the Bill. I am not clear about many of the points that have been gone over to-night. If Mr. Drayton, the chief man in the Immigration Branch, were here, he would probably be able to give the minister the information. For instance, what is meant by ' municipal purposes?' Then, I am hazy about section 6. I have not the slightest suspicion of its being wrong, but it requires some little study and explanation. The right seems to be taken here that the minister may, whenever he considers it expedient, waive the necesssity of public notice for filing the memorial or the memorial and plans. The footnote says this is necessary in comparatively trivial cases where the water is required for washing gravel or taking out ice. That qualification, however, is not in the section of the proposed legislation. I would like to know more particularly the answer to the points I have raised. In Moosejaw, for example, we have had quite a municipal problem. A year ago last winter a company was engaged in taking out ice where it always has been taken out, and all of a sudden an injunction was taken out against them by the Canadian Pacific railway. It appears that the Canadian Pacific railway had some old water licenses for damming the water for their railway operations; and, not for the sake of all the ice which they could take out, but for other reasons, they wished to put a block in the way of these men, and took advantage of this Act to stop them by injunction. A very great wrong might have been done to the city, and possibly was done for all I know, by puAting the ice trade into the hands of a nonopoly. They made it possible to take ice from a pond

a mile long. Some powers should be taken by the Government to grant relief against any arbitrary assertion of rights that go to the grantee of a water license. I mention that because the explanatory note refers to the cutting of ice.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman's suggestion that the minister should give an explanation of the whole Bill is a proper one, as the second reading took place by consent and without the usual explanation. I may be able to make this section clear by reading subsection 1 of the present Act, which is as follows:
In the case of applications for water for domestic or irrigation purposes, the minister may, if he sees fit, waive the necessity for filing the plans required by this Act, and may require the applicants to file a memorial only.
It is proposed to amend that by striking out the word ' irrigation ' before the word * purposes,' and then the subsection would be as follows:
In the case of applications for water tor domestic or other purposes, the minister may, if he sees fit, waive the necessity for filing the plans required by this Act, and may require the applicants to file a memorial only.
Then there is section 2, which is not touched:
The minister may order that such memorial shall contain all the information necessary to a full and complete understanding of the rights applied for.
The third subsection as proposed, is set forth in the Bill. This section had better stand until the minister comes.
Section stands.
On section 7-S. 29a amended:

If the explanation in the footnote explains thoroughly, there seems to be no objection to this section; but I would suggest that, instead of the section being drafted as it is, the old section should be repealed and a new section substituted conveying in so many words exactly what the intention is. It makes it much more simple, and I think is better in every way.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend's suggestion is carrying out a principle that I have advocated a great many times myself. I think it is the better way to carry out an amendment in most cases.

It is for laymen; I do not know how it is for the men of the law.
Section stands.
Progress reported.

tell my hon. friend. I have no knowledge of one of our inspectors going down there, but I will make inquiries.

The papers are making

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

We are not authorized
under the Act to deal with horseflesh.

Notwithstanding the lateness of the session and the amount of legislation we have on hand, I am sure that if there is a business enterprise in Montreal such as my hon. friend mentions, the House will agree to spare the time to pass legislation authorizing the Minister of Agriculture to take the necessary steps.

There are two of these
enterprises in the county of Chambly. The horses are bought at from $8 to $20 a head, and some of them can hardly limp to the abattoir to be knocked down.

La Patrie has a story about it to-night.
' Mr. MARCIL: They claim that the meat is exported to Sweden, but we have no guarantee that such is the case.
I think the minister will realize that this is an emergency.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When the Agricultural Estimates were before the House on the 26th February last, there was some discussion with regard to the purchase, or 220i
rather the non-purchase, of a property in the county of Carleton for an experimental farm. The hon. member for Carleton made some remarks which reflected on the conduct of two gentlemen ih that county, and suggested that the reason the property was not bought in Carleton county was that ii it had heen a rake-off would have to be paid to Mr. B. P. Smith. I will read what my hon. friend from Carleton said:
I want to make a correction in the statement I made before dinner, because I want the record to be correct in every way. I said the minister had an offer from Mr. Charles L. Smith to sell 500 acres of land in Woodstock-the very best land that could be required for an experimental farm, including all grades of soil for $20,000. I am wrong in that. I think the offer the minister has in his department is $30,000. The difficulty was that another gentleman, this time the postmaster at Woodstock, Mr. Norman W. Winslow, was the medium; he was the commission merchant in this case. Mr. Winslow, and as he stated, my opponent, Mr. B. J. Smith, had to have $10,000 as a rake-off, and therefore if the farmer wanted to sell his farm he was compelled to put the price at $30,000 so that the politicians could get $10,000 as a rake-off; he would get but $20,000 for his farm. These are the facts of the case.
I do not propose to enter into any discussion of the matter, but I have been asked by Mr. Winslow and by Mr. Smith, both of whom are reflected on by this statement, to place side by side with that accusation against them the statements which they make in regard to the matter. On the 28th February I received this telegram from Mr. B. F. Smith:
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa, Ont.
Referring to the discussion in the Commons on the twenty-sixth instant, as reported in Hansard, regarding the purchase of land in New Brunswick for experimental farm, cowardly allusions made to myself by F. B. Carvell are absolutely false in every particular. Would ask for an investigation.
B. F. Smith.
Later on, Mr. Smith wrote me a private letter dated March 4, but in a subsequent letter, dated March 6, he asked me to read his letter of March 4 to the House, as he has nothing to conceal. This letter reads as follows:
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Ottawa, Canada.
Dear Mr. Hazen,
With reference to the statement which appears in ' Hansard,' made by Carvell, regarding the purchase of land in New Brunswick for experimental farm. I beg to say that the statements, so far as I am concerned, are false, in every particular. I cannot see why he should be allowed to get by with that kind of talk. The files of the Minister of Agriculture will show that I never recommended the purchase
I am afraid that the gentleman referred to by my hon. friend, Mr. Winslow, has been in so many little land deals around Woodstock since he became postmaster.
Is he the postmaster of Woodstock ?
Yes, he is the postmaster at the present time.
What does the Postmaster General say about that ?

The Postmaster General does not care as long as it is a Tory who is doing these things, Mr. Winslow has stated that he was acting for Mr. B. F. Smith. I make no reference now to what Mr. B. F. Smith may have said. But my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries very kindly told me that he had received letters from Mr. Smith and Mr. Winslow which he wanted to read to the House, and, without giving me copies of the letters, he told me that they claimed that the difference between $20,000 and $30,000 included in some way the Upham farm. Inasmuch as the matter might come up in a day or two, I wired to Mr. Smith the general result and I received this letter from him which I purpose placing upon ' Hansard.' Fortunately I have something else beside this, which, I think, will convince the minister that his friends in New Brunswick are very badly muddled over this real estate transfer. I will read the letter first.
What Mr. Smith is this?

This is Mr. C. L. Smith, who owned the farm in question:
Woodstock, N. B., March 9, 1914. F. B. Carvell, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Out.
Dear Frank:
At your request about the selling of my property for an experimental farm.
Mr. Holyoke, a real estate man of the town of Woodstock, told me that he wanted my farm for an experimental farm as the Government was going to have an experimental farm in the province of New Brunswick. I gave him a price of $20,000 for my farm, Including the Upham interval.
I hope you will remember that Upham interval and Upham farm are two different transactions entirely. The Upham farm originally was^one of the oldest grants on the river St. John, and next south of it was the Smith farm, or the Smith grant. Some years ago, the Upham interval, consisting of about one hundred acres on the Lont of the Upham farm, was sold to Mr. C. L. Smith, who thus owned not only the Smith homestead which had been in the family for 125 years, but the interval in front of the Upham farm.
Afterwards, I was sent for by Mr. Winslow, postmaster of the town of Woodstock, and he made the same request. I told him that Mr. Holyoke was ahead of him. Mr. Winslow said

that Mr. Holyoke could not put the deal through, as he (Mr. Winslow) had B. F. Smith with him.
Mr. B. F. Smith is the gentleman who now controls the patronage of the county.
Mr. Smith having the patronage of the county, and being with Mr. Winslow, I told Mr. Winslow to go ahead that I wanted to sell the farm. My price was $20,000 including the Upham interval, and I did not care which one sold it. Mr. Winslow took the matter up and Mr. Grisdale of the Department of Agriculture was sent here. I was told by Mr. Winslow that Mr. Grisdale would he here, and that I was to ask him $30,000 for the farm of 400 acres, at $75 an acre, including the Upham interval.
Tours truly,
(Sgd) C. L. Smith.
As far as that goes, we simply have the word of one man against another. I would not have made this statement had I had nothing else than simply the ordinary gossip that may go around the neighbourhood, but I have always tried to back up with documents any statement that I have ever made in this House. I have knowledge obtained from a source which, I think, will satisfy even the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that I was justified in making this statement.
During the summer of 1913 a railway company required a certain portion of the Smith farm for right-of-way, and as they could not agree upon the price it went to arbitration. I was Mr. Smith's solicitor and counsel, and naturally Mr. Smith was trying to make his farm as valuable as he could, because like every other landowner he felt that great damage was being done him, and as the value of the farm played some part, it became important, in my opinion, to show the arbitrators everything that could be shown to give them an idea of the value of the farm and the consequent damage caused by the taking of the right-of-way; this being a stock farm and the pasturage being behind the railway. I have here the record of the case which was decided on sworn testimony. Before I had any idea at all of what Mr. Winslow or Mr. B. F. Smith was going to say, Mr. 0. L. Smith, the owner of the farm, gave evidence as to the value of the property. I read from page 29 of the case, part of the evidence of Mr. C. L. Smith:
Q. In your opinion how much will the building of this road across the land as you have described depreciate the saleable value of your property?-A. I say $4,000. I wouldn't have it there for $4,000 if I want to stay there and farm.
Q. Have you had any offers for your farm of late?-A. Yes I had an offer this spring in writing, and one last June, I think.

Q. From whom?-A. Mr. Winslow, postmaster.
Q. Norman Winslow?-A. Yes.
Q. How much?-A. $20,000.
Q. For your whole farm?-A. Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
With the railway there
or not there?-A. They would have whatever they got from the right of way.

Did you have any other
offers?-A. Well parties had an option last June for $30,000.
Q. Who did?-A. Mr. Winslow, $75 an acre for 400 acers. No writing about it but he was to have the land for that amount.
Q. Then he came back this year and offered you $20,000?-A. He did.
Q. Did you accept his offer of $20,000?- A. I told him at first that-I didn't understand that he wanted the whole thing, and when he wanted the whole 600 acres I wouldn't let him have it.
Q. How much did you suppose you were offering to sell for the $30,000?-A. The same as a year ago.
Q. How much?-A. 400 acres.
You have there the sworn testimony of Mr. C. L. (Smith given in a case, in which this matter about the $10,000 rakeoff played no part whatever, and he said he offered his land to Mr. Winslow for $30,000, including 400 acres.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Was there any agreement in writing?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Where does he say that?

He says that in the
letter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That statement is not contained in the evidence.

The statement is contained in the evidence that he asked $30,000 for 400 acres, and that 400 acres included his main farm and the Uham interval. Mr. Winslow sees the difficulty he is in and he says now that the $30,000 offer was on account of the George W. Upham farm, but that >farm never was mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: How do you know?

I know it was not because I have the sworn evidence of Mr. C. L. Smith. I will tell my hon. friend more than that. I will tell him that George Upham would be insulted if any one went to him .and asked him to sell his

farm for $9,000 or $10,000; he would not sell the remainder of his farm for $15,000. When Mr. Winslow talks about the George Upham farm being included it is a pure fabrication. Mr. Upham is a client of mine; he was also in the courts and we fought out the matter, and we won, I am happy to say. I would know i(f. George Upham ever had any offers for his farm. There is not .a particle of this gentleman s business for the last ten years that I have not done for him. My own personal knowledge teaches me that the George Upham farm never was mentioned, and never was dreamed of until this matter was brought up and the postmaster saw he was in rather an unpleasant position in Woodstock, and then he writes this letter to the minister, dragging in the George Upham farm in order to account for the $10,000 rakeoff. I do not want to discuss this matter any further in the absence of the gentleman, neither of whom are here, but I think I have given sufficient evidence-the sworn testimony of Mr. C. L. Smith 'before thi3 matter was eveT thought of-to show that the offer he made to (Mr. Grisdale for $30,000 included only the 400 acres of his own farm, and that George Upham's farm never was thought of. I appreciate the position in which Mr. Winslow is. I know that this thing created certain consternation in Woodstock, because a great many people, Conservatives as well as Liberals, believed that if it had not been for the attempt to make a rake-off we would have had the agricultural farm in Woodstock instead of in Fredericton. Naturally, when the matter became known, a good deal of adverse comment was made on it and these gentlemen down there, seeing the box they were in, attempted through the medium of the minister-who I admit is perfectly innocent in the matter-to square the thing and make an explanation, but fortunately we have the sworn evidence of a court of record, given eight or nine months before this thing took place, entirely disproving the whole story. I would say, as a word of advice to my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen), he ought to know both these gentlemen well enough to be a little cautious how he reads letters or telegrams from either of them, to substantiate any proposition which looks a little fishy upon its face.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is perfectly clear from what has been stated that my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) has no charge to make against Mr. Frank Smith in connection with this
matter. As the matter appeared on the records of this House, after the statement made by my hon. friend on the 26th of February, any one reading that would come to the conclusion that Mr. Frank Smith, who has been twice a candidate in the county of Carleton, was a party to an arrangement by which an endeavour was being made to obtain a rakeoff of $10,000 on the sale of his farm. The statement of my hon. friend shows that there is absolutely no evidence; that there is absolutely nothing that resembles evidence, to justify any such charge against Mr. Frank Smith. As far as Mr. Smith is concerned there is nothing whatever to in any way reflect upon his conduct in regard to this matter or to show that he had any connection with it in any way whatever.
In regard to the other matter, it would appear from these proceedings, as we have them here to-night, that it is a question of credibility as between Mr Winslow on the one hand and Mr. C. L. Smith on the other.
Sworn testimony.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Mr. C. L. Smith I know
well, as I also know Mt. Upham and Mr. Winslow well. Knowing Mr. Winslow as I do, I desire to say that I do not believe that Mr. Winslow would deliberately make a statement that was not true in connection with this or any other matteT. I have known him for a great many years and that is the opinion I entertain of him. My hon. friend says there is sworn testimony, but that sworn testimony of Mr. Smith was given in connection with another matter altogether when this question was not under consideration. The only statement to the contrary is that made by my hon. friend, that he has been Mr. Upman's solicitor for years and that, if any such offer had been made, he would know about it.

Does Mr. Winslow
state in his letter that Mr. Upham came to him and offered to sell his farm for $8,000 or $9,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is what I understand.
It is simply preposterous.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend may state that it is preposterous. I think I am stating the matter correctly.
I will prove that it is preposterous.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend may say
that it is preposterous; but my hon. friend was not there. He does not know; he simply says that nothing of this sort could have occurred, because he has been for a good many years past Mr. Upham's solicitor, and therefore he would have known. I do not think that is a logical deduction from the fact that my hon. friend has been Mr. TJpham's solicitor. Mr. Upham might very readily, in connection with his property, have made in the course of conversation offers of which my hon. friend is not aware. Apar.t from that altogether, if we are to believe Mr. C. L. Smith's evidence given at the time as to the. value of the right of way running across his property, we have the statement made ;by Mr. Smith that there was an option on the property, but that that option was not in writing. In that case it would not be an option at all; it would not have the slightest bearing and effect in law if it had not been reduced to writing and signed by the different parties to the agreement. The option, if we call it an option, is simply a verbal one; there is evidence that there had been a conversation between Mr. Winslow and Mr. Smith with regard to this property; and the matter having never been reduced to writing, no contract having ever been entered into, it seems to me it is easily within the range of probability that there was a misunderstanding between these gentlemen as to what the oiler was for, or as to the amount of property embraced in the offer. Under the circumstances, it may be that each gentleman is honestly telling what he believes to be the facts with regard to the matter. We all know that in conversations of this sort, which are not reduced to writing, what mistakes occur, what misunderstandings take place. As I said before, while I am very glad to hear to-night that my [DOT] hon. friend practically exonerates Mr. Frank Smith from any connection with the matter; I might also say that having known Mr. Winslow since we were boys together,
I do not -believe he would make any statement that was not a true one with regard to a matter of this kind.

I think I stated in the beginning that I had no evidence that Mr. Frank Smith was implicated, except what Mr. Winslow told Mr. C. L. Smith. I think my hon. friend will find that I made the statement in February that Mr. Winslow said that Mr. Frank Smith was in it.

I did not state that Mr. Frank Smith was in it; I simply stated that Mr. Winslow said that he was. If my hon. friend can take any satisfaction out of that, I gladly give it to him; but I do not want to make any statement or claim about any gentleman at all which might injure him, without being able to prove it to the hilt.
When I come to the Winslow part of the matter, I cannot be so charitable. It is true that my hon. friend says that we have not any evidence here except a verbal statement of one gentleman against the other, and he rather tried to get behind the technical side of it and stated that it was not an option because it was not in writing. I am not arguing that it was a legal option; I am only stating the facts of the case. Mr. Grisdale will be able to tell the minister, if he will ask him, that Mr. C. L. Smith demanded $30,000 for 400 acres of his farm. Mr. 'Smith swore that he was willing to take $20,000 for it. As my hon. friend seems to have such a high opinion of Mr. Smith, and says that this $30,000 offer included Mr. Upham's farm as well, I do not think I am to be blamed if I give a little professional information I have on this matter. Within half an hour after that offer of $30,000 with $10,000 rake-off was made, I was consulted professionally about the matter. I told Mr. C. L. Smith that he was very foolish to be mixed up in any such transaction, because it would lead only to a scandal, and that I thought he had better write a letter to Mr. Grisdale stating that he would accept $20,000 for his farm. I wanted an experimental farm and I did not want any boodling out of it either. If my hon. friend wants an affidavit as to that fact, I can easily get it from the gentleman who gave it to me. I know what I state here is a fact, namely that Mr. Upham's farm was never though of in connection with the matter. All this talk about including the Upton farm to make up the $10,000 is a pure fabrication.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can only tell my hon. friend that, knowing Mr. Winslow as I do, I will unreservedly accept his statements about the matter, until the contrary is proved.

Knowing him as well
as I do, I will place no confidence in him at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend
will place more confidence in Mr. C. L. Smith.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I would like to say to my hon. friend, 'because be made the statement before, that the minister had in his possession an offer of $30,000, $10,000 of which was to be a rake-off, that I have looked into the whole matter and I have no offer whatever on the Smith farm.
It was made to Mr. Grisdale personally.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
What conversation may have taken place between Mr. Grisdale and Mr. Smith I do not know anything About. As to any offer being made to the department, there is no offer at all in the records.
In regard to this item, I might state very briefly how it is made up, so that the hon. members of the committee will be informed. Somewhat over $40,000 of this is planned to be expended, as it has been in the past, in connection with the various winter shows throughout the provinces, including also all the judges of the different shows, whose expenses we pay, the fat-stock shows and stallion shows of each province. The record of performance work is estimated to take about $21,000. In that we have a number of men employed, the breeds of cattle being the Holstein, Ayrshire, Jersey, French Canadian and shorthorn, of which a record is being kept by our different inspectors. The sheep branch takes about $10,000. The poultry division takes about ,$20,000. I shall be very glad to deal with any of the matters that my hon. friends wish to know about a little later on. Then, there i's the horse industry, which takes about $80,000 or $90,000 this year. As regards this, I would like to say a word of explanation to the committee, because it is somewhat of a new departure.
Hon. gentlemen will probably remember that there was a good deal of criticism last year in regard to the action of the department in giving a bonus of $250 apiece for thoroughbred stallions, and it was thought to be somewhat of a discrimination .against other breeds. . On going into the whole matter and studying it as closely as we could in the department, we came to the conclusion that we had better adopt a different system this year. Accordingly we propose to adopt, in connection with this part of the appropriation, a system somewhat similar to that carried on in England and Scotland, with which system some of my hon. friends are probably familiar.
The conditions relating to horse breeding that at present obtain in Canada seem to
warrant the conclusion that the time is opportune for the breeders in each municipality or district to adopt more freely cooperative measures in providing for themselves the service of suitable stallions. It is generally admitted that improvement in breeding methods can be effected most rapidly and conditions permanently remedied by organized effort on the part of the owners of mares. In the past a number of breeders have, by their energy and enterprise, aided greatly in the advancement of the industry, and they deserve every credit for the splendid service they have rendered. Unfortunately, these men have been comparatively few in number and the business has not progressed, therefore, as rapidly as could be desired. It is now felt that by judicious and systematic assistance horse breeding as an industry can be greatly stimulated and benefited. Except in the more favoured districts, improvement in breeding practice has been hindered hitherto through the lack of such concerted action as would enable the farmers to procure and retain the services of good breeding sires. In a majority of sections, breeders wishing to grade up their horses are forced to use whatever stallions may by chance stand for service in their district. Many of these are faulty in conformation and lack in quality, while others, though of better type, remain, either through insufficient patronage or because of failure to leave colts, but a single season in each district. The fact also that there has been no systematic adherence to the use of one breed suggests another reason for the lack of progress in the breeding of high class animals.
It must be recognized, further, that the owner of a valuable horse, after paying for maintenance, insurance, interest on investment and the expense entailed in the collection of his fees, has frequently little left from his outlay, particularly in districts where he has to compete with grade and scrub stallions standing for service at a very low fee. As a result, really high class stallions can be maintained only in districts where the breeding of horses has been given serious and progressive attention. In view of these considerations it is proposed to enter upon a policy which may serve to place the horse breeding industry in Canada in a position comparable to that which it has attained in Great Britain and other European countries. It is believed that by encouraging the organization of breeders' clubs and by enabling such clubs to procure the services of good breeding stallions
Is it the policy of the department to discontinue the bonus?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes-discontinue it to
one special breed, but applying this method to all breeds, believing that it will have in the long run as beneficial effect upon thoroughbreds as upon other breeds, and put the whole on a fairer footing.
Will that interfere with the remount policy of which the Minister of Militia spoke?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Not necessarily at all.
Because, as I understand the proposal,-

though I would not undertake to discuss it at this time-it is not finally decided, or if it is decided I would prefer that the Minister of Militia should discuss it. I understand that it is left open for the Government to purchase from any farmer as before.

I am sorry the Minister of Militia is not here; but this matter can be taken up again. I understood this breeding ranch will be handed over to the National Bureau of Horsebreeding. And I understand that the National Bureau, the owners of this ranch, undertake to purchase the progeny of these ibonused thoroughbred stallions and develop them on the ranch. I think that the doing away with the bonus might interfere with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: Would the minister state what price he paid for the horses he purchased from Mr. Lane?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

I know Mr. Lane's stud of horses very well. He has imported some of the very best Percheron horses that could be purchased in France, and when he took that price for these horses he sold at a very great sacrifice. I know that for the past five or six years he has been selling these home-bred Percheron stallions at from $1,000 to $1,600 each. I have bought a horse from him for which I paid $1,600. I think it was simply his

public-spiritedness that induced him to sell these stallions at that price. He did it for the purpose of keeping out inferior low grade scrubs that would have been brought in had he not agreed to sell those horses to the department, and I think it was an act of very marked public spiritedness on his part. I am very much surprised to hear that he would accept that price.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is well to hear that there are public-spirited men who will sell at a sacrifice for the public good.

When this item was up last year I did not offer any criticism.

I felt ut the time that it was best to await the practical working out of the policy. My reason for offering a few criticisms tonight is that I have had quite a lot of letters from breeders and farmers in the West pointing out that the policy is not at present satisfactory. I do not wish to be misunderstood and so I would point out that I am not opposed to the farmers of the West, or even of the East, if they cannot get good sires, receiving Government aid. But I think there is a better method than the purchasing of these Canadian bred sires. I think that the maximum price is $600. I do not believe that a stallion, suitable for a sire, can be bought for that price. Pehaps it is possible just at the present time, tout in past years it would not have been possible because I find that the Ontario breeders and breeders from south of the line have brought a great many stallions into Alberta and Saskatchewan in the past eight or nine years and they have been selling those horses, in some cases for cash in other cases on two or three years' credit at prices ranging from $1,500 to $4,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Prices on the average
horse, as my hon. friend knows, have decreased quite a lot.
Mr. WARNOCK; I have quite a number of cases in mind where they sold as high as $4,500. We have had in the past altogether too many low grade stallions in the western provinces. I think the hon. member for South Ontario will agree with me in that. We have altogether too many low grade stallions, and I think the federal Government is doing a good deal towards perpetuating the use of these low-priced horses by our farmers. The provincial governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and, I think, Ontario are doing everything in their power to discourage the use of these low grade stallions. In some of the provinces the stallion ordinances have recently been made very rigid and I know that in Alberta it is proposed to take steps, perhaps at the next session of the Legislature, to amend the stallion ordinance and make it much more drastic. The minister has said that his department proposes to purchase Canadian bred sires. I do not quite understand how that would effect the proposal to have a community system.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
I do not think they would conflict at all. We are not going to purchase the stallions at all. That will be a matter for the clubs or associations. As some farmers are not in a position to pay

for the use of a first-class stallion, we are offering to pay to these clubs twenty-five per cent of the fee to encourage the farmers to patronize the best horses.
Would that twenty-five per cent be paid to the executive of the association?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: To the secretary.
Not direct to the stallion's owner?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No, the association would have to pay him.
Why would not the horses bred from imported sires be as good as the sires imported?

I will explain to my hon. friend. My experience has been-and I think it is the experience of every breeder
in Canada-that in order to keep the progeny up to the standard of excellence you must, from time to time, import pure bred stock from the land of origin of these animals, whether it is horses, cattle, sheep, hogs, or any other kind of live-stock. You must get in fresh blood. I think every breeder in this House will agree with me on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend agree that it would be better for the individual breeders to import stock for their own establishments?

quest the Hon. Martin Burrell, Dominion Minister of Agriculture, not to distribute any stallions in Alberta.
That resolution was passed almost without a dissenting voice on the 13th April, just about the time of the Calgary spring show.
Then, I have an excerpt here from a paper published in my own constituency, the High River Times, a paper which is not at all unfriendly to the present Government. I presume the editor penned this after the meeting of the Calgary Stockbreeders' Association. It is as follows:
Discouraging Breeders.
If the Dominion Department of Agriculture had for its object the improvement of livestock throughout the country they have evidently missed their mark. During the past year many stallions and bulls have been shipped here in Ontario, and placed in different communities where the homesteader had the privilege of using them. The idea would be a popular one if the class of stock being distributed were as good as Alberta bred and stock from the old country. There has been better stock imported into this province during the last ten years than in any other part of Canada, and it is to be regretted that importers and breeders of Alberta should be so discouraged m the laudable work in which they are engaged.
We understand that $600 is the highest price the department officials will pay Alberta breeders for their pure-bred stallions, and as a result very few choice animals are obtained. The outcome is that an inferior class of breeding stock is being distributed among the farmers. As an evidence of the unpopularity of the move, we may cite the instance of the horse breeders' meeting last week at Calgary, where practically every man present opposed the scheme.
Is the Horse Breeders' Association of Alberta not largely composed of the importers of horses?
All the members, perhaps, have imported horses, hut a number of them have imported horses for their own use, <not for sale. Others are both importers and breeders'.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I would like to say very frankly that I could read scores and scores of resolutions from aJil over the West conveying a diametrically opposite opinion, but I do not want to go into a controversial discussion to-night. I think that my hon. friend's own criticisms are very fair, but when it comes to statements of this kind it must 'be' Temembered that sometimes resolutions are engineered and sometimes there is a misunderstanding as- to the work that is being done. I do not think that statement reflects' the general opinion off the people of the West.

Of course, the policy
has not been very long in vogue I want to be fair. I am referring to draught stallions. With bulls 'and rams any harm that may be done by a poor sire is very soon eliminated by sending the animals to the block as soon as they are in condition. But it is a different thing with a house. I have seen tery few of the sires sent out by the department, hut this year I intend to see as many as possible and form my own opinion. I believe that the minister will give my suggestions a little thought. I hope he will agree with me that the policy of bonusing good, heavy draught sires in the way that the department Rais been bonusing thoroughbreds in the past will be of far greater benefit to the horse-breeding interests of the West. I have no objection to the bonusing of thoroughbreds; we have a great scarcity of saddle horses and drivers in the West, but if the thoroughbreds should be bonused, the good heavy draught sires ought to be bonused as well.

In Tegard to this
question of assistance to better stock breeding, I would like to say to the minister that in my province, as in most of the eastern provinces, we have had for a long period of years a system of agricultural societies in which men meet together and, with a good deal of public spirit, devote themselves to the improvement of stock. I would like to point out to him in all kindness that in dealing with this question of the improvement of stock he ought to utilise this condition. I was very much surprised-personally I do not Tegard it as of any political significance or as being a disadvantage to me politically-to find that the Conservative local member for my constituency, during the winter, was writing letters to the newspapers announcing this policy of my hon. friend and putting it on as if it were some political arrangement. Letters from my county are to the effect that Conservative farmers are grouping themselves together and applying to my hon. friend to get a bonus for the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We are not carrying it out along those lines.

That is what is going on. I do not regard it as being of any political disadvantage to me because any one foolish enough to be engaged in that silly business would not he elected in the constituency I represent. If the minister is really desirous of making the proposition

a success in our province, we have these organizations that have gone along entirely on non-political lines where men have worked together for the general benefit and if he is in a position to utilise these local agricultural societies he might supplement what is being done by the various provincial governments. Imported stock has been brought into all the provinces in the East, and, in connection with these agricultural societies, there has been a great deal of stock improvement. I think that the minister, if he would act along these lines, would be able to accomplish some good results by supplementing the efforts of the provincial Government.
I take advantage of this opportunity to call the minister's attention to another matter. A -friend of mine, Mr O. S. Campbell, K.C., of Montreal, has been largely interested in horse breeding. He is a well known gentleman who for a long time occupied a high position at the Bar. Becoming interested in the breeding of horses he has devoted himself to matters in connection with that line. He had some correspondence with the minister in regard to the matter. This correspondence was brought down in response to a motion for a return. Although I do not profess to be anything in the way of an expert in regard to this question, the correspondence which he had with the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Agriculture discloses what I think is a very ,grave defect in regard to the importation of pure bred stock into this country. The minister is familiar with the customs regulation which provides that no thoroughbred stock can be imported for the purpose of improving of stock breeding unless it is accompanied with a certificate from the National Association of Canada or some other association of like standing. Last year Mr. C. S. Campbell communicated with the Department of Customs in regard to this matter and stated that it was his desire and intention to bring in a thoroughbred mare from the United States. He wanted to bring her in free of duty. He wrote to the department for information and they sent him a copy of the customs regulation. I quote from his letter:
I am advised by the accountant of the National Live Stock Records at Ottawa that the American studbook of thoroughbred horses does not come within the list of recognized thoroughbred records, and I infer from his letter that the English, French, and Australian studbooks would come under the same ban.
If that statement is correct it seems incredible that some Canadian organization should undertake to decree that the certificates or studbooks of every English, French, Australian or American Association of horse-breeders would not be sufficient to permit entry into Canada of a thoroughbred horse free of duty. He goes on to say:
I was under the impression that the amendment to the regulations had been made with the object of facilitating the import of thoroughbred horses, but if books such as the English, American, and Australian Studbooks, which are recognized all over the world, are not placed by the National Record Committee in the class of books of record recognized as reliable, it is obvious that the importing of thoroughbred horses has not been made any easier by the amended regulations.
1 would be obliged if you would let me know whether it is the intention of the Customs Department, under the authority conferred by the minister as to the forms, that a British subject who presents at a port of entry an animal unquestionably thoroughbred, and who also presents registration certificates from such a book as the English, or American studbook, and makes the affidavit required, should be prevented from getting his free entry by the fact that the National Records Committee declines to certify that the English and American studbooks are recognized as reliable authorities.
To that letter my friend Mr. Campbell received the following from Mr. Me-Dougald, the Commissioner of Customs:
In reply I am to state that under the regulations as formulated by the Government regarding free importation of animals for the improvement of stock, it is necessary on each importation to furnish a certificate stating that the animal is recorded in the Canadian National Records or in a foreign record recognized as reliable by the National Records Committee.
Of course, that left the matter as it was, and apparently Mr. Campbell approached the Department of Agriculture, and it does not appear from this correspondence, but from what he tells me personally, he has not been able to get any change from that interpretation which, to use his own language, puts under the ban the certificate from the English, Australian and American studbooks. He writes to the Minister of Customs, and, after referring to the fact that he had received this letter from the Commissioner, he says:
It appears that I am by the Order in Council entitled to enter an animal duty free if I furnish an import certificate stating that the animal is recorded in a Canadian National record or in a foreign record recognized as reliable by the Canadian National Record Committee.
This proposition seemed to me to be absolutely fair and calculated to remove some serious difficulties that lay in the way of importers under the previous regulations. It never oc-cured to me, nor do I believe now, that it was the intention of the Government in passing the Order in Council that I should be placed in the power of the National Record Committee to-

exercise its duty of recognizing a foreign record as reliable or refusing it as a mere instrument to obstruct the importation of stock.
Probably ninety per cent or more of the thoroughbred stock in Canada are registered in the American studbook, a book which is recognized as reliable throughout the civilized world. Those who do not trace to this book, trace to the British studbook, a book, if possible, of still higher standing.
The Canadian Thoroughbred Register, which seems to be controlled by the National Record Committee, takes up the pedigree of an animal out of the British or American studbook and continues it, and it is inconceivable therefore that in good faith the National Record Committee could refuse to recognize the British and Amerian studbooks as reliable.
On application, however, to the accountant of the Canadian Live Stock Records, he advises me as follows:-'The accompanying booklet, (a pamphlet printed by Taylor Brothers, Queen street, Ottawa, Canada, 1913) beginning on page 37 shows a list of Canadian books of record, and beginning on page 39 is a list of recognized foreign books of record, consequently the American studbook does not come under the list of recognized foreign records.' A very widely signed petition was sent to the Minister of Agriculture from this district, signed by importers and breeders of thoroughbred stock, and by members of the Montreal Jockey Club representing that the difficulty of getting thoroughbred stock were enormously increased by the obstacles that were placed in the way of the would-be importer by the then existing regulations, and it has been understood that the new Order in Council was intended to accede to their wishes and to enable the purchaser of a thoroughbred animal abroad to bring it with certificates which showed it to be a thoroughbred to the port of entry and there to fmter it free of duty if the certificate was the certificate of a reliable foreign book of record, the importer making affidavit as to the identity of the animal.
You will see that the present attitude of th [DOT]National Record Committee makes such i system impossible and remits the importer ti the same position of difficulty that he stood ii before the new regulations.
My friend Mr. Campbell also addressed the Minister of Agriculture and practically at the^ same time he received a letter from the Minister of Customs acknowledging the receipt of this letter and stating that his letter had been transferred to the Minister of Agriculture. He wrote the Minister of Agriculture in the following terms, under date 30th May, 1913:
Montreal, May 13, 1913.
The Honourable,
The Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ont.
Sir:
I have the honour to enclose you herewith for your information copy of letter sent by me this day to Mr. D, Macrae of Guelph, a director of the Canadian Thoroughbred Horse Society.
It struck me as peculiar that a gentleman in Mr. Macrae's position saw no further into the question than to suggest that a difficulty about the fees was at the bottom of the discussion.

Anybody who knows Mr. Campbell knows what a splendid personal character he is and how truly unselfish he has been in regard to this question of stock, and indeed in every walk of life, and they will agree that for any one to think that he was quibbling about a question of fees is simply ridiculous. The letter continues:
I have been at some pains to endeavour to make it clear to him that this is not so, and it occurred to me that it might be advantageous to importers in this province if you had the same information before you.
I am to-day in receipt of a letter from the accountant of the Canadian National Live Stock Records which I frankly confess I am unable to understand. The Order in Council certainly^ grants free entry to animals that are recorded in the Canadian register or in a register recognized as reliable by the National Record Committee. This committee's accountant writes me 'It is not within the jurisdiction of the Record Committee to say in connection with the issuing of import certificates for free customs entry that the English, French, American or Australian Thoroughbred Studbooks are recognized foreign records. The reason of this is that these records are taken care of by the Canadian Thoroughbred Horse Society.
Upon what authority the National Board Committee can transfer its authority to the Canadian Thoroughbred Horse Society, I do not know. Colonel Hendrie, president of the society, admits that his register is obstructing duty free importations. If the National Record Committee has abdicated its functions and allows its accountant to remain under the impression that the business is to he taken care of by the Canadian Thoroughbred Horse Society it is quite easy to see how and why my importations are obstructed and also to make it clear that except action be taken by yourself I shall be left without any other remedy than to pay the duty and endeavour to recover the cost of it from Mr. Brant.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
C. S. Campbell.
The Minister of Agriculture is familiar with this matter, and all the correspondence I need not read in detail. But finally on the 30th of July last year Mr. Campbell wrote to the Deputy Minister of Agriculture:
I have parted with ' Long Ago,' the mare I had in the States, and have made arrangements to return ' Brynwood ' to the States. Will you kindly, therefore, return me the certificate I sent you in mine of July 8.
So far as I can see it the situation is such that there is no inducement to attempt to bring in new stock and a great many reasons for not attempting it, and as without new stock the possibility of meeting the American competition on an equal footing is taken away from us, I have concluded to give up breeding in Canada.
Mr. Campbell is a son of Sir Alexander Campbell, former Minister of Justice of Canada. Mr. Campbell is animated by the highest motives, and no one would think of

attributing to him any selfish idea in regard to the matter. Having leisure and means at his command, he laudably, with the idea of improving horse-breeding in Canada, entered into importing thoroughbred stock and raising thoroughbred animals. When he did so he found that by the operation of the Order in Council, when he went to England and when he went to the United States and got mares or stallions, the status of which was recognized by the studbooks of those countries, and brought them into Canada, he could not get them in free of duty, and was thus debarred from the encouragement which the country ought to give to the importation of stock of that kind. As a consequence, after going into horsebreeding for a year or two, he went out of it altogether. Not being an expert in this business and not speaking from that stand point, but having heard Mr. Campbell's story personally, having read his correspondence, knowing that there is no possibility of misrepresentation so far as he is concerned, I think that, if the condition of affairs, as asserted by Mr. Campbell, exists in Canada to-day, it is the duty of the minister to remedy it. I would like to hear from the minister his explanation of the case made out by Mr. Campbell in these letters; and whether or not, if that condition exists, he cannot by an amendment to the Order in Council provide some remedy so that a man who wants to do what Mr. Campbell evidently wanted to do may not be prevented-by some arbitrary and foolish regulation from doing so.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is a pretty familiar
subject; and, as my hon. friend knows, and probably some other hon. members know, the brief that he has given to the House now on this matter is of precisely the same character as that placed in the hands of Senator Casgrain and read in the Senate a short time ago.
I did not know.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes. The whole matter has been gone into just as fully in the Senate; and as a result of that, a special committee of the Senate has been appointed to thresh the matter out in detail, and witnesses are to be summoned. At all events, Mr. Campbell is to be given the fullest opportunity to come here and have the matter gone into thoroughly Whether or not he has availed himself of that opportunity, I do not know. I would not like to go into the whole story. I quite agree 221
with my hon. friend that we are not disputing Mr. Campbell's honesty of purpose in this matter; but it is a case where one particular view has seized his mind and the department holds another view and we -cannot see eye to eye. I believe that Mr. Campbell, in his desire to get animals in here free of duty, has refused to conform to certain regulations, amongst which are that, when we have in Canada a national record system for any particular breed, an animal of that particular -breed that is imported, has to be registered here. As I understand it, Mr. Campbell will not do that. I might also point out-I think I am right -in this: I shall be corrected probably by my hon. friend if I am wrong-that the Government of the United States would not allow a man to bring an animal from this country duty free into the United States, unless it were registered in our Canadian record of that particular breed, whatever it m-ight be.
There was another very strong grievance of Mr. Campbell, namely, that he did not want to conform to our regulations, because they required that when a man imported an animal from the United States, he had to furnish a certificate of identity so satisfactory that it had been backed up by the transfers -showing the number of hands through which the animal had passed. It i-s particularly desirable that this should be done, because there are a great many horses syndicated in the West that have been brought in there ostensibly with certain registration -certificates which -can sometimes be -obtained pretty easily; people have been gulled; and no responsible party -can be got hold of -should the animal prove to be absolutely worthless. I think my -hon. friend (Mr. Warnook) w-ill bear me out in that. There has been a very strong request from every one interested -in the horse industry to have a system of identification so complete that the horse industry in this country will be thoroughly -covered. In some of these matters Mr. Campbell did not see eye to eye with the department. I do not profess to have sufficient legal training -to see all the fine points -of the matter; but the conclusion come to by myself and toy the officers of the department who were interested was that we could not take any action.
Mr.. MACDONALD:	I do not profess to
be an expert on this matter; but, on reading these- documents, it strikes me as an anomaly that there -should be any authority in Canada that will say: You can not



regard an animal coming into Canada as being thoroughbred in the sense that it may be imported free of duty, although the animal has a certificate of the English or the American or the Australian register. Why should not such a certificate toe sufficient?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: That is not altogether the po:nt, although it may be one point. The policy has been laid down that Canada is now b.'g enough and important enough from a breeding standpoint to stand on its own feet and to have a national record system of its own. It is to the interest of ever}' one who wants to benefit by bringing in a breed of any kind to have a Canadian reg:ster of that particular breed. If a man gets a horse of a particular breed from somewhere else, he must have it registered on our Canadian books as well. On that point, however, my hon. friend from South Ontario (Mr. Smith), if I am wrong, will be able to put me right. The subject is a rather involved one.

In the first
place, I wish to congratulate the Department of Agriculture upon the way in which the live-stock industry is being managed at the present time. A great deal of life has been thrown into the Department, of Agriculture within the last few years, which I think is having its effect upon the breeders and farmers of Canada from one end of the country to the other.
As far as the objections raised by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Warnock) are concerned, I would say that, whilst he was very moderate in his expressions- and I would, expect that from a gentleman of his standing and of his knowledge of Northwest conditions-I cannot altogether agree with him. In the first place I take it that the object of the department is to supply outlying districts, namely, where Canadian bred horses are being used and travelled, as is done in many places in the [DOT] West and in Ontario. Price does not mean everything in connection with a horse of this description, so that I do not think a great deal of harm can be done. There is this to be said, namely, that the policy of the Government is helping the farmers and the breeders of that class of horses, and they are getting a fair price for them. Therefore, I would scarcely believe Mr. Lane, as I know him, to be actuated altogether by sentiment in selling his colts for $600 each. In regard to the resolutions that were read,-1 think I see the hand of 
an old and prominent breeder of the province of Alberta. I refer to Mr. John A. Turner. When representations were made to Mr. Lane after the sale was effected, complaining that he had made it, his answer was that he was running his own business and running it in his own way. If the policy of my hon. friends opposite were carried out, instead of breeding these horses by our own people in the different provinces, the matter would be transferred altogether to another country, and there would be no object at all in a breeder crossing an animal so that it could be recorded in our registers, because there would be no special sale for such an animal. There animals have to be bought for Ontario in Ontario as long as they last; for Alberta, out of the province of Alberta; for Saska'chewan, the same, and so on in the other provinces. If there is not a sufficient number in a province, then the perple can go outside the provinces in order to get the balance.

When there is a good
imported horse in the district, would not my hon. friend believe that that horse might be used without bringing in an outsider if arrangements could be made with the owner?
If I understand the policy aright the department would not send a horse to a section where there was already an imported horse.

I think that for this
year in a portion of the district south of Macleod application has been made for a stallion. I understand they wanted a Percheron, but they were informed by the department that a Percheron could not be sent, but the department could get them a Clyde. I believe there is a very excellent imported horse in the district, and I know that within thirty miles from Macleod there are a number that could probably ibe got for a small bonus added to the fee.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

speechtext: I assume that. But the policy is not being carried out quite in the way the minister has indicated. In that Macleod district I want them to get a good stallion and not have some scrub sent in there, because there are a lot of valuable mares and it would be regrettable to have a scrub sire get into the district.
Does not he propose to record it when it comes in?

No, that is one of the difficulties. One of the very strong positions taken by every association is that every animal must be identified. Mr. Campbell says that that is an utter impossibility. But we do not have any other record, finding fault or complaining. We say that unless every animal is identified, we lose the goodness of our records. Take, for instance, the Thoroughbred Association, of which, no doubt, at one time, he may have been a member. The matter was brought by Mr. Campbell before that association, of whieii Mr. William Hendry was the president.

Colonel William
Hendry, of Hamilton?

Yes. In connection with that I wish to read Colonel Hendry's reply, which covers the whole ground:
The executive committee are fully advised as to the situation and the determined efforts on the part of Mr. C. S. Campbell to obtain his object through channels which might only inform your department of Mr. Campbell's side of the situation. I, therefore, was instructed to write you a personal letter giving you the personal view of the officers of the society. Briefly, the position is as follows: It is well to remember that when the society was formed, and when it was made a national one like other

breeds of live-stock, all the prominent breeders were in favour of the change, some of them largely interested and who had been both breeding and racing for many years before Mr. Campbell became identified m a similar capacity. Therefore, at this stage, why should not the past experience of these gentlemen and those comprising the society to-day, be of sufficient importance to warrant the affairs of the society being properly conducted? Mr. Campbell desires to have the privilege of bringing his animals into Canada 4 free of duty,' without recording such animals in the National Live Stock Records and paying the recording fee in the Stud Book of same. If his ground is well taken and his action supported by those in authority in your department, or any other department of the Government, then the whole system of importation of pure bred live-stock Into this country is nullified, and the breeding interests will receive such a setback as they will never recover from.
Mr. Campbell has stated in a letter to me that the society seeks to put obstructions in the way of importing into this country, pure bred live-stock. This is a serious charge, and one which, as president of the society, I desire most strongly to disagree with. On the other hand, if your department were to follow the advice of Mr. Campbell^ and some others from his province, the absurdity of his contentions would only be exceeded by the serious damage it would do to the breeding interests, not only of all breeds of horses but of other live-stock breeds.
The Record Committee published a list of Canadian records and all information pertaining thereto, and a list of recognized foreign records in their annual report which is spread broadcast to breeders, and may be obtained by any one else who may apply. Many foreign records, while on the list of recognized records issued by the United States Government, are not recognized in their entirety. An importer cannot tell whether animals are entitled to free entry into the United States until their pedigrees 9-re passed on by the authorities at Washington. While, generally speaking, all thoroughbred horses are admitted free to the United States, the Jockey Club, New York, practise a system of protection by making registration in their book compulsory within a certain period by a fine of $100. Transfers mean a chain of title to prove identity and prevent fraud by substitution. There has never been any difficulty with horses from Great Britain, as the Stud Book authorities in England issue an export certificate for all animals leaving the country, which absolutely proves his identity and ownership.
The first customs regulations in reference to the free importation of animals for breeding purposes came into effect on October 1, 1870. As to identification of animals, they .were as stringent as those of the present time. In the case of a thoroughbred horse, a certificate of purity of blood, a certificate of identity signed and sworn to by the importer and a certificate of registration in either the English or American book was required.
The National Record Board exists by an agreement with the Department of Agriculture.
The Record Committee has never declined to perform the functions delegated to it.
The Government, by incorporating the Cana-
IMr. Smith.]
dian Thoroughbred Horse Society, does not delegate to the National Record Committee authority to say whether the English, American, Australian, French or any other stud book is reliable.
The Customs regulations memo. 1713b and 1750b plainly state that if there be a Canadian record for the breed an animal must be entered therein.
An importer, before purchasing, can obtain from the National Record office information as to the eligibility of any animal.
Transfer of title is necessary to prove identity. The basis of all reliable records is the. transfer of animals when sold. Without transfers you might as well accept every man's private record and abandon National Records.
No difficulty exists but with horses from the United States. The American Thoroughbred Stud Book does not enforce any system of transfers. The American Stud Book has been described as having a foundation of sand. Only horses that are noted performers on race tracks can be identified by race track officials or race track followers. Canadian purchasers of American horses on American tracks are in tho same position as American purchasers of Canadian horses on American tracks. Canadian registration is required for Canadian horses entering the United States free of duty. It is doubtful if it is not illegal to change to a free entry for breeding purposes, a race horse that is under bond to be returned to the country from whence it came.
Most British and continental records were established because of exportations to foreign countries, principally to Canada and the United States. American records were established in many cases prior to those in the country where the breeds originated.
The National Record has passed the experimental stage. The paid membership reaches almost 10,000 persons and the number of people doing business with the National Record office is probably 35,000.
Pedigree registration is mostly based on honesty among breeders. The honest breeder insists on the most stringent regulations for his protection.
Animals already in the country at the time of inception of any record have the same system of identification applied to them as those that may come in later.
The progeny of unidentified animals upon which the duty has been paid, cannot be recorded.
If a mare is brought into the country in foal, is unidentified and duty paid, the foal cannot be registered until the mare is identified.
This pretty plainly shows the work of the Record Board and of the Record Committee and what is demanded. If any one thing was given up in connection with thoroughbred horses and their registration, everything in connection with it might as well go. There must be the identification of the animal in every case.
Progress reported.
